BURTON MEYER, Jr.

BURTON MEYER, Jr.
Grand Master
October 17, 1974 - October 16, 1975

Our l09th Grand Master served the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free
and Accepted Masons of the State of California during its !25th anniversary
year.
His charm and good humor have endeared him to Masons and their families
both within and without this Grand Jurisdiction.
Known affectionately as "Burt, " our Grand Master was born February 12,
1921 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. At a very early age he and his family came to
Oakland, California and by age IO they had settled pennanently in Los Angeles .
There he was educated in the public schools and attended Los Angeles City
College.
Burt allied himself with the printing industry at a very early age-from a
paper route as a young boy, rising through the ranks as pressman, salesman and
finally (and currently) owner of a successful finn-Bookman Press in Los
Angeles. He is a Past President of the Printing Industries Association of Southern
California.
This detennined but steady rise in his profession had several interruptions in
his early years.
He served in the Forestry Service and had some active duty in fire fighting.
The War years (World War II) found him serving a six-year enlistment in the
United States Coast Guard-rising to the rank of Chief Boatswain' s Mate.
He served in the Pacific, the Atlantic (including the invasion of North Africa)
and finally on an ice-breaker off Greenland and Iceland .
He concluded his active service in the Coast Guard in recruiting. His public
speaking ability was recognized and used by the government for he appeared in
person and on radio in War Bond drives.
He married Diane Lee in 1946 and has had the full support and cooperation of
his dear wife.
His Masonic career began in 1945 when he became a member of Golden State
·
Lodge No . 358, having been raised a Master Mason June 29, 1946.
Not content in being "just a member" he embarked upon a career devoted to
service in Masonry-ultimately becoming Master of his Lodge in 1960.
His service to Masonry includes membership in both the York and Scottish
Rite Bodies.
In the York Rite our Grand Master is a member of Inglewood Chapter No .
131, Royal Arch Masons; a member of Alpha Council No. 39, Royal and Select
Masters and a member of Santa Monica Commandery No. 61, Knights Templar.
In the Scottish Rite, Burt is a member of the Los Angeles Bodies in which he
was invested as a Knight Commander of the Court of Honor in 1959 and was
coroneted an Inspector General Honorary 33° in 1965. He served as Wise
Master, Chapter Rose Croix, in 1965-66 and as Venerable Master in 1972. He
now serves as Chainnan of the Inspector General's Advisory Conference for
these bodies.
Our Grand Master also is a member of Al Malaikah, A.A.0.N.M.S.; a
member of Saint Gabriel Conclave, Red Cross of Constantine; a member of the
iii

Royal Order of Scotland and served as President of the Robert
the Bruce
Association in 1975.
Because of his exemplary concern for our nation's youth and particul
arly the
young men of DeMolay, Burt was awarded the DeMolay Honorary
Legion of
Honor Award in 1970 and was elected to honorary membership in the
International Supreme Council , Order of DeMolay, in 1975.
Our Grand Master is a great humanitarian, and his concern for the welfare
of
others is exhibited in his membership on the Board of Directors of the
Midnight
Mission, which Board he serves as its Vice-President. He also demons
trates this
humanitarianism through his service on the Board of Governors of
the Shrine
Crippled Children's Hospital (Los Angeles unit).
But even all these activities do not fully tell of our Grand Master's service
to
Freemasonry.
His service to the Grand Lodge of California began with his appoint
ment to
the Correspondence Committee in 1959 and again in 1960. He is the
representative of the Grand Lodge of Japan in California. In 1961 he was appoint
ed an
Inspector, which post he faithfully served until he was appointed Assista
nt Grand
Lecturer in 1966. Zealously and diligently discharging the duties of this
office he
was appointed Grand Orator in 197 l and his fervent orations thrilled
audiences
throughout the jurisdiction.
The Brethren in this great Fraternity recognized the calibre of Burton
Meyer,
Jr. and elected him Junior Grand Warden in 1971. This election
started his
progress through the progressive elective line culminating in his election
in 1974
to the highest office the Fraternity can afford- Grand Master of Masons
.
Our Grand Master has exhibited all of the traits of character which make
him
the sort of man others are proud to call "brothe r."
He is patient and calm. He is empathetic for he responds to the needs
and
feelings of others. With all his charm and wit, he is resolute, positive
and
courageous. His Brethren have found him to be both dependable and coopera
tive.
In short, he is all, and more, that a Grand Master is expected to be. The
nurture
and care of Masonry in California has been in good hands during his
tenure as
Grand Master. Most Worshipful Burton Meyer, Jr. -our Grand Maste
rWe Salute You!!

Invocation
Almighty God, our Heavenly Father, we thank Thee for the many blessings
we have received from Thee this year. For Thy watchful care over us in our many
travels; for the brotherly love we have experienced; for the inspired leadership
our Grand Master has provided; for the loyalty he had engendered and for the
individual acts of kindness. And, 0 God, though our paths may soon separate
may we remember these acts of goodness and helpfulness we have expressed one
to another. Grant in Thy mercy that our paths may cross again. Until then, may
the warmth of a handclasp, the union of spirit with spirit remain a beautiful
memory until we are joined again in that house not made with hands, eternal in
the Heavens. We pray in Thy Holy Name. Amen.

Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of Grand Lodge:
A long time ago, before the debates on fire-arms, when my sons were still
young, we enjoyed going to the police rifle range. We had a twenty-two caliber
Stevens rifle and we had a very good time. There came a time when the boys
discovered that I had a revolver. This had been given to me while I was doing
some work with a Police force. The revolver was beautifully engraved
to
commemorate their gift to me. Having discovered that I had a revolver the boys
began a systematic campaign to have me bring the revolver to the range. I made
excuses but it was to no avail. The boys were assured that I was a champion with
a revolver. I finally gave in and took the revolver to the range. I could no longer
resist their demands to show them how well I could shoot. So, we asked for
the
right target, at a right distance, and hoping that I would at least hit the target,
I
fired. The boys and I peered at the target but we could see no mark. We asked
to
see the target at close range. Finally we spied the mark. Not along the edges
where I had been looking, but right in the center of the black bull's eye! "Do
it
again" the boys shouted. "Absolutely not" was my reply. So the boys loved
to
talk about my shooting skill.
I was younger then, much younger. I was wiser then, much wiser. Once
before I stood at this lectern, that was in 1971, and delivered my message to you.
You flattered me with your kind response. After that experience I should have
said, "Absolu tely not!" But when I was asked to repeat, I forgot my target
experience. I said "Yes" when possibly I should have said, "no." But how very
pleasant it is to stand in this place and bring another message to you.
I certainly extend to the Grand Master my sincerest appreciation for having
asked me to repeat. The lapse of five ·years has given me an even greater
appreciation for our beloved order and my travels with the Grand Lodge Officers
a new regard for those who give so very much during "their year."
Recognizing the importance of this occasion I will do my best to bring to you
the kind of message these moments merit. This is not an easy task. It calls
for
much self discipline. Very often when a fine audience, such as this has gathered
there is a great temptation for a speaker to voice a pet theme or advance some
deep personal desire or ambition. I battled with the same temptation as your
Chaplain in 1970-71. Since I truly believe that a Chaplai n's message should
be
more than a fine oration and since I believe the spiritual nature of our Order
should be the focal point of this message, I read again a list of my duties as
I
found them in an old ritual. This is the charge: "Revere nd and Worship
ful
Brother, that Book which is the chart and textbook of your sacred calling, is also
the great light of Masonry and forever sheds its benignant rays upon every lawful
assembly of Free and Accepted Masons. Teach us from its life giving precepts
;
intercede for us with the Divine Majesty which it so fully unfolds and reveals
to
us; and warm us with its lessons of infinite wisdom and truth, and you will have
faithfully performed your sacred functions and fulfilled your important trust."
What other admonition could I have hoped for, and what could define more
clearly my duty and my privilege for this morning. Hear again the three points:

I. Teach us from its life giving precepts.
2. Intercede for us with the Divine Majesty.
3. Warm us with its lessons of infinite, wisdom and truth.
Now, with this as a guide I could blot out all other voices and temptations
for
popular and exciting topics.
. .
.
.
For many of us this travel through life has been, and st1ll 1s, a very mterestmg
experience. Many of us would, as a contribution for many favors, leave some
memento of our being here or having been here.
It is possible that, somewhere along the way, we may have been able to erect
a landmark of whatsoever nature. Possibly an actual "footpri nt on the sands
of
time." Such an ambition is certainly laudable. I am often impressed reading
the
obituary of a dear friend and I say: "I knew him so well, for so many years and
still never knew his accomplishments. What an interesting individu al."
Some of us because of the roles we play, may have been forced to reveal
some of our ow~ private life and our ambitions. While ~his has been a~l too ~e
in
my life, I have had one experience which I have only hmted at from time to ~1me.
Always there has been the dread of being misunderstood and the. expenen
ce
remained unmentioned. This morning I would like to open a door a httle farther.
I do have an experience to relate which, at some time, may be of help to you.
Then too if I were to choose an audience for this "confes sion" I could hardly
choose a better one. Possibly that is why I have not spoken of this before. Suffice
it to say that I had reached a period in my life when death seemed to be far more
desired than a continuing life. The situation I faced appeared so hopeless and I
so
very helpless. Everything for which I had worked and. had dreamed,
my
reputation and my good name seemed on the verge of sacnfice. There was
no
human to whom] could turn. I thought of a very fine attorney, a Mason, whom
I
respected, and I wondered what he would do in my circumstance. I knew
he
would tum to his God. I decided that I too, without any intermediary, would tum
to that source of help and strength.
The memory of this conviction is very clear. I closed the doors to ~y ?ffice
when, without any pre-planning, I found myself on my knees. Now, this is not
my usual attitude in prayer. I had often wondered why some people knelt. I knelt
in prayer as a child and I knelt in prayer in the Lodge. Now it became very clear.
Circumstances compel one to such action. It was in this attitude that I app~ach
ed
the throne of God with my supplication. There was no great burst of hght,
no
thundering words, just a great calm, a certainty that my words had been heard.
I
thought of the Psalmist's words; "Be still and know that I~ God." I repe~ted
this many times and gradually the words seemed to mean: Stop your fighting,
be quiet, be relaxed, let all fears pass, leave this to God." To act out these words
was not easy. I also wondered whether I was going through an emotion
al
experience, a religious experience or a spiritual experience. I learned that in truth
this was a spiritual experience.
That evening I wrote the Psalmist's words on a small scrap of pa~r ~d
placed it into a small envelope. Old and brown and discolored as you see it, this
envelope is one of my cherished possessions. This was. only the begi~ning of
the
"miracl e." As I meditated on that which was happening another Bible passage

Devotional

8

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

came to my mind. I repeated it as I remembered it: "Be not afraid, I am with
you, I am your God, I will help you, I will strengthen you, I will walk beside
you, touching your right hand saying, I will help you." The effect of this was
extreme. Until the end of the experience, which lasted more than a month, I
seemed very conscious of the presence of God, touching, as it seemed, the
promised hand of God. These things I noted and placed the notes into the little
envelope. Then as if in answer to my thought, "Why is this happening to me,"
there came a third Bible passage: "We know that all things work together for
good to those who love God." On a little memo pad I wrote: "I love God and I
am grateful for all He has done for me. Certainly, since He has demonstrated His
care to this time I can expect His continued blessing and help, even though things
do look dark." My great trouble seemed to be that I felt that there was something
more that I should do. I had not learned that I "must wait a time with patience."
Into the little envelope went these words: "God moves in a mysterious way
His wonders to perform. Today is the day of the Lord." In spite of all assurances
great doubts still filled my days. Then, in a remarkable way a great miracle came
to pass! Then I added a final note to my envelope: "Surely the Lord was in this
situation and I knew it not.''
This was an actual happening. I bring it to you as factual with the hope that in
some mysterious way, you too, at a crucial point in your life, may benefit from
this spiritual experience. Do you wonder then why I, when faced with today's
assignment, had little choice but to bring this message? I have chosen for a topic
these Masonic words: ''Divine assistance is vouchsafed.'' To this I would add; in
times of great and extreme anguish, when human help fails, I will:
1. Stop fighting and place my entire trust in God who said: "Be still and
know that I am God."
2. Stop fears, for there is assurance of help: "Fear not for I am with you. I
am your God, be not dismayed I will strengthen you. I will support you, touching
your right hand, saying I will help you."
3. Since I love God I may claim the gift for such love: "All things work
together for good to those who love God."
4. After the experience we can say: "Surely the Lord was in this (place)
situation and I knew it not.''
A German philosopher advanced a most interesting thesis. He said, in effect,
when you are reasoning, it is not always necessary to begin with an established
fact. Begin with a doubt, with an "as if." By this I understand him to mean,
begin with a doubt and then act as if this doubt were true. Many examples come
to mind. There must be thousands of people driving cars who know nothing
about the mechanics of the car. They only know a few essentials. They turn a key
and the motor starts. They shift gears and they are off, entirely ignorant of why
these things happen. They act "as if' or as though they knew. We turn a switch
or press a button and our house is lighted. Thousands of times daily we use
equipment we do not understand, but we act as though we knew, and things
happen. How impossible our lives might be if we could only use things we
understand. We can apply like standards to our spiritual life and call "as

if'-"Faith!" I cannot explain the miracle I have related . By taking the course
which I took and believing, having faith, amazing results followed . If we had
only half the faith and belief in things spiritual as we have in things material we
might in truth be able to move mountains. "Divine assistance is vouchsafed" we
are taught. Hold fast to this truth.
You who have listened to my remarks have your own concept of: "Supreme
Being." To some this may relate to an anthropomorphic God, to others the
concept expressed in the words: "Wherever I am God is." You will be correct, if
in your own light you understand that which I endeavored to portray.
"Be still and know that I am God."
"Fear not for I am with you."
"All things work together for good to those who love God."
"Surely the Lord was in this incident, and I knew it not."

Necrology
Again, we have reached the hour when we pause to remember our Masonic
Brethren who have had a divine summons and have passed beyond the portals of
our human Lodges since· last we met and to pay our tribute of respect and
affection to their memory.
"In the beginning, God created the Heavens and the Earth, and the Earth was
without form and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the spirit
of God moved upon the face of the waters, and God said, 'Let there be light,' and
there was light.'' ''And God formed Man out of the Dust of the Earth; and God
breathed into his nostrils the Breath of Life, and Man became a living Soul. God
appointed that Man should not live forever, but that he should come to the end of
his days, and h\s Soul should return unto Him Who spake it into existence."
In Masonry, we are also reminded of the brevity of life and the inevitableness
of death. The "Hour-Glass," an emblem of human life, reminds us "how
swiftly the sands run and how -rapidly our lives are drawing to a close." Man
wastes away. "Today he puts forth the tender leaves of life; tomorrow blossoms
and bears his blushing honors thick upon him; the next day comes a frost which
nips the shoot; and when he thinks his greatness is still progressing, he falls like
autumn leaves to enrich mother earth." Or "behold what havoc the scythe of
time makes among the human race." We must soon be cut down by the
all-devouring scythe of time, and be gathered into the land where our fathers
have gone before us .
As we walk in memories' hall, we recall the many virtues of our departed
Brethren and grieve for the fellowship that we shall enjoy no more. Some have
served as business, civic or community leaders; some in government, some in the
military, others in the field of education, the judiciary and many other vocations,
but most of all we honor them for their labors in the vineyards of Masonry.
It is the duty of this Committee to report on our deceased Brethren who have
passed away during the fiscal year 1974-75.
The statistics of our report are somewhat overwhelming. None of us will
know all on that roll, but all of us will know some of the names, and some of us

IO

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

will recognize many names of long time friends and Brothers with whom we
have worked and had rich fellowship. The compilation of the list is always a little
saddening. "We long for household voices gone and for vanished smiles, but
God has lead our Brethren on, and He can do no wrong." Time will permit
the recitation of the history of only a few, yet all are worthy. Their individual
names and Lodges will be inscribed in the printed record of our Annual
Communication.
During the past year four hundred ninety-six (496) of our Members were
translated from this imperfect Lodge to that all perfect, glorious, and Celestial
Lodge above where the Supreme Grand Master forever presides. Two hundred
sixteen (216) of our Lodges suffered losses. Two Lodges lost five (5) each; seven
Lodges four (4) each; twenty-eight Lodges three (3) each; ninety-five Lodges two
(2) each; and eighty-four Lodges lost one (1) each.
Among the departed was our well known and beloved Past Grand Master
L. Harold "Pete" Anderson who was called to the Supreme Lodge on high on
October 16, 1974. He was made a Master Mason in Palo Alto Lodge No. 316 and
served his Lodge as Master in 1942. He was appointed Grand Sword Bearer and
then to the Board of Control. There followed eight years as a Trustee of the
Masonic Homes before being elected Grand Master in September 1956. He was a
member of the Scottish and York Rite Bodies and Islam Temple of the Shrine,
where he served as Potentate in 1953. After his term as Grand Master, he
returned to the Masonic Homes where he provided great leadership as President
of the Board. He was also designated to the Legion of Honor, Order of DeMolay.
The eulogy for Brother L. Harold Anderson will be given by a very dear and
close friend, the Right Worshipful John F. Roberts, Jr., Deputy Grand Master.
James Edward Hammond-P ast Master, was Master of Park Boulevard
Lodge No. 568 in 1927, and served as an Inspector of the 36th Masonic District
for 10 years. His firm of Certified Public Accountants were auditors of Grand
Lodge and Masonic Homes accounts for many years. He also served as a member
of the Grand Lodge Committee on Taxation until he retired.
William F. Traverso-Pa st Master and a Mason for fifty-three (53) years. In
1927 he was Master of Roosevelt Lodge No. 500 (now consolidated with Golden
Gate Speranza Lodge No. 30). He served on the Charters Committee in 1934 and
on the Constitution Month Observance Committee in 1946, 47 and 48. He spent
all of his adult life in the legal profession. Recognizing his talents Past Grand
Master Earl Warren, the then Governor of California, as his first judicial
appointment in 1943, appointed him to the Municipal Court Bench. In 1945, he
was named to the Superior Court where he served until his retirement on March
26, 1965. It is said "that the benc.h and bar lost one of its ablest jurists."
George W. Burch, Jr. -Past Master of La Brea Lodge No. 650 where he
served as Treasurer for sixteen years. He was elected to and received the rank and
decoration of Knight Commander of the Court of Honor in January 1956 and
coroneted a 33rd degree Mason on December 9, 1961 in the Los Angeles Scottish
Rite Bodies. He was a member of the Committee on Jurisprudence in 1951 and
since that time served on the Committee of Correspondence and as its Chairman.

He was a diligent worker on the Grand Lodge Publication, The California
Freemason .
Alfred J. Mccourtney -Past Master of Lancaster Lodge No. 437, an educator
in areas related to law. He served Grand Lodge as a member and Chairman of the
Grievance Committee from 1964 and was appointed to the Jurisprudence
Committee in 1974. He also assisted the Committee on Code revision. He had 19
years of Judicial experience, serving as Judge of the Municipal Court for 8 years
and Judge of the Superior Court since that time. In 1971, he ·was elected
Assistant Presiding Judge of the Superior Court and elected Presiding Judge in
1973. In 1975, he was appointed to the District Court of Appeals. Brother
McCourtney was a Member and Chairman of many Judicial Committees and
Councils and named "Judge of the Year" in 1974. He leaves an enviable record
in the field of Jurisprudence.
Samuel Roy Howell-"R oy," Past Master of Henry Knox-Westlake Lodge
No. 392 and Officers' Coach. He was a member of both the York and Scottish
Rite Masons and Al Malaikah Shrine. His ardent work with the Los Angeles
Scottish Rite Bodies, among which was the Class Room, earned for him the high
honors of a 33rd degree Mason. He served Grand Lodge as a Director of the
U.C.L.A. Masonic Club House for many years.
David H. Blakelock-P ast Master, San Clemente Lodge No. 671 and served
as its Master in 1956 and Treasurer for 9 years. He received the coveted 50 year
Pin in 1967. He was appointed Senior Grand Steward in October 1962 and served
as Chairman of the Sojourners Committee in 1963, 1964 and 1965. He was a 32
degree Scottish Rite Mason and a Member of Honolulu Aloha Shrine Temple.
Active in military affairs, he participated in the atomic bomb testing at Bikini,
transportation, a Logistic Officer and as Commanding Officer. He was a
Brigadier General at the time of his retirement. He was very active in charitable
organizations and civic affairs. He served as Councilman and Mayor of the City
of San Clemente during the years 1954 to 1962. He was named "Citizen of the
Year" in 1974.
Stanford Fong-Past Master of Justice Lodge No. 549, served as Officers'
Coach a number of years. He served as a member of the Public Schools
Committee in 1965 and served as a member of the Credentials Committee during
the years 1971, 1972 and 1973. He was appointed Grand Bible Bearer in October
1973. Brother Fong was a Knight Commander of the Court of Honor in the San
Francisco Scottish Rite Bodies and a member of Islam Temple of the Shrine. He
was a Past President of the Chinese Acacia Club.
Richard H. Dutwiler-Pa st Master served as Master of Atwater Lodge No.
622 in 1961. He was appointed to the Public Schools Committee in 1964 and
served as its Chairman until 1973.
Daniel D. Rowlands-P ast Master, was Master of Mt. Davidson Lodge No.
481 in 1952. He was appointed Inspector of the 340th Masonic District where he
served with distinction until his appointment to the Committee on Distribution in
1971. He was appointed Grand Bible Bearer in 1972 and then in 1974 served on
the Commercialism Committee.

David Wright-w as raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason in
Corinthian Lodge No. 22 in Canada. He became a Plural Member of Paul Revere
Lodge No. 462 and Menlo Park Lodge No. 651. In 1955 Brother Wright was
appointed the Grand Pursuivant. Three years later the then Grand Master, Phil N.
Meyer, in 1958 appointed him Grand Tiler where he served for many years. In

Between Temple Associations and Constituent Lodges. He was appointed to the
Endowment Board in 1969. In 1974 he was appointed to the Library Committee.
On March 9, 1972 he became eligible to receive the Fifty Year Veteran Button
award.
Victor N. Hodge -an athlete, coach and educator served as Master of San
Bernardino Lodge No . 348 in 1934. He was Secretary of his Lodge for almost 25
years and the prime moving spirit in the planning, fund raising, building and
dedication of the beautiful San Bernardino Masonic Temple. He was a Charter
Member and First Secretary of the San Bernardino Scottish Rite Bodies and
presented an award as a 50 year Scottish Rite Mason on April 12, 1972.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

13

EULOGY
LoUIS HAROLD ANDERSON

By John F. Roberts, Jr.

L. HAROLD ANDERSON
Grand Master - 1956
BORN
March 29, 1899
St. Cloud, Minnesota

DIED
October 16, 1974
Palo Alto, California

Affectionately known as "Pete" to his many, many friends, L. Harold
Anderson was a big man in every sense of the word. He lived his 75 years to the
fullest. Whatever he strove to do, he attacked with vigor and enthusiasm-play
as well as work.
Having had the exceptional opportunity of chauffering him to and from Palo
Alto and San Francisco for the ten years immediately prior to his retirement in
1964 as Vice President and Assistant General Manager of Pacific Gas and
Electric Company, and since then attending many board and committee meetings
with him, I had a rare opportunity to become very well acquainted with "Pete."
He had a rare sense of humor which never left him. I remember some time
ago that he gave a tie as a Christmas present to one of his close friends. The tie
was a railroad tie that Southern Pacific had discarded. Even a very few weeks ago
when he was so seriously ill in the hospital and very anxious to go home, and
finding that his clothes were not immediately available, said, "I guess I'll have
to streak out of here."
"Pete" had a tremendous capacity for work. His great energy and ability are
emphasized by the work he was carrying on during his year as Grand Master of
Masons in California and Hawaii in 1957. He fulfilled all Grand Lodge
commitments while giving daily attention to the important requirements of his
vocation as Vice President and Assistant General Manager of P. G. & E. All of
this was done while meeting the demands made upon him as a member of the
Advisory Board of the Bank of America, Palo Alto Branch; Director and Vice
President of the San Francisco Downtown Association; member of the Pacific
Coast Electrical Association; Pacific Coast Gas Association; American Water
Works Association; and both the United States and San Francisco Chambers of
Commerce.
Since his retirement from P. G. & E. in 1964 he has been active on several
boards and important committees. As a member of the California Masonic
Homes Board, he has done a great deal of work in investigating the suitability of
its present site and in planning its redevelopment. As Vice President of the Palo
Alto Masonic Temple Association, he has had much to do with the planning and
financing and building the beautiful Masonic Temple in Palo Alto at University
A venue and Florence Street. He was very active in helping handicapped people
to find gainful employment and quietly performed many acts of kindness for
friends and acquaintances.
"Pete" was a devoted family man. He was very proud of his sister, Mrs. Al
Larson, who traveled all the way from Minneapolis, Minnesota to sing for him at
an important event. He was extremely devoted to his wife, Edna Mae, and to his
two daughters, Mrs. Anna Louise Ashford of Salem, Oregon, and Mrs. Nona
Lucille Wells, of Oceanside, California. I remember the show of affection when
I was present on one of his birthdays when several of his nine grandchildren sang
"Happy Birthday" to him over the telephone.

14

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

What virtue unites, death cannot separate. Our Beloved Brother L. Harold
"Pete" Anderson, has left a heritage to us that time can never erase.' His smile
his helping hand, his kind word-these are holy acts, the memory of which
transcends .from this world to infinity. He who loved, cared and helped has
beco~e a~ imm~i:tal as the spirit of love, compassion and charity. Thus, though
we miss his famihar features, he is not now, nor ever, any farther away than our
own hearts.
We shall ever cherish his memory.

PAST MASTERS, MASTERS AND WARDENS
OF CONSTITUENT LODGES

"So~t.and Safe ~o thee, my Brother, be thy resting place! Bright and glorious
be thy i:ismg from it! Fragrant be the acacia sprig that there shall flourish! May
the earhest buds of spring unfold their beauties o'er thy resting place, and there
may the sweetness of summer's last rose linger longest! Though the winds of
autumn may destroy the loveliness of their existence, yet the destruction is not
final,. and in the springti~e, they shall surely bloom again. So, in the bright
mommg of the resurrecuon, thy spirit shall spring into newness of life and
expand in immortal beauty, in realms beyond the skies. Until then, dear Brother,
until then, farewell."

JOHN MILLS BROWNE-GIFT JEWEL*

A Century ago, in 1875, John Mills Browne was elected to serve the Masons
of California in the exaulted station which you now occupy. He was re-elected in
1876-1877 and 1878, the last Grand Master to serve four terms.
Brother Browne was not only a most distinguished Mason but was also a
noted Naval doctor. Spanning a forty year career, Brother Browne rose from
Assistant Surgeon in 1853 to Surgeon General, the highest medical rank in the
Navy. He served as the first Medical officer at the newly established Mare Island
Navy Yard at Vallejo in 1854, served actively on shipboard during Naval
engagements during the Civil War and retired with the rank of Commodore in
1893.
In addition to this outstanding Naval Career, John Mills Browne's service to
Masonry is equally outstanding. He received his blue Lodge degrees in Philesian
Lodge No. 40 of Winchester, N.H. in 1852 while a Medical student at Harvard.
He affiliated with Naval Lodge No. 87 in Vallejo in 1866 while stationed at Mare
Island Navy Yard and became Worshipful Master in 1871. He was appointed
Grand Orator of the Grand Lodge of California in 1871, elected as Junior Grand
Warden in 1872 and progressed through the chairs of the Grand Lodge until
elected Grand Master in 1875. He found time to serve some 18 years in various
offices of both the York and Scottish Rite in California and for his signal service
to Masonry he received the 33° of Sovereign Grand Inspector General from the late
Alfred Pike.
John Mills Browne lived for only a year following his retirement, dying in
1894 in the Nation's Capitol. He is buried in Arlington National Cemetery.

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

125TH ANNIVERSARY GAVEL

OPENING REMARKS

On October 17, 1974, at the Installation of the Grand Lodge Officers, I was
presented with a beautiful gavel and sounding block to be used during the 125th
Anniversary year of the Grand Lodge of California. This wonderful gift was
made by Brother William Smith, member of Palo Alto Lodge No. 346. The hand
crafted gavel and sounding block depicts the history of Masonry in California and
is inscribed with many historic emblems. Made of redwood burl, it is truly an
historical gavel and one that will enjoy fame in the history of this Grand Lodge.
The gavel has traveled the length and breadth of the juristiction and has been the
center of attraction wherever it was displayed. Your Grand Master and the Grand
Marshal have carried this gavel and sounding block, in its beautiful traveling
case, to nearly every Grand Lodge event during 1974-1975.
I express my deep thanks and appreciation to Brother William Smith for this
wonderful presentation.

"Far away, there in the sunshine, are my highest aspirations. I may not reach
them, but I can look up and see their beauty, believe in them and try to follow
where they lead."
With this quotation, we started our new Masonic Year. I am sure that each
Grand Master has delivered his message at the conclusion of the year with mixed
emotions, with the feeling that many tasks were not completed, yet filled with the
knowledge that he tried to do his best.
My Brethren, I look back on the many pleasant memories that this past
Masonic year has afforded me . I want each of you to know how proud and
pleased I am to have had the opportunity to serve the members of our great
Fraternity as your Grand Master. Your friendship, extended to me throughout
this jurisdiction, is ample reward far beyond that which I could ever have hoped
for or expected. I am humbly grateful for this, a never to be forgotten experience.
In every way I have endeavored to serve you and our Fraternity with whatever
abilities I possess. Whether or not I have been able to accomplish this remains to
be seen. In the final analysis the Masters, Wardens and Past Masters are the
Grand Lodge of California, and you are to be the judges. Be compassionate in
your understanding and charitable in your evaluations.
ST ATE OF TIIE CRAFT

With very few exceptions, Masonry in California is on a sound foundation. A
few incidents caused your Grand Master concern. Fortunately, these were
resolved and peace and harmony prevails.
Decisions and recommendations covering the incidents that could not be
resolved under our present laws are contained in this message.
This year has been devoted to the Masonic youth groups-DeMolay, Job's
Daughters and Rainbow for Girls. I have stressed the importance of every Master
Mason in California providing strong and dedicated leadership for our youth. The
future leaders of our Nation must be inspired by Masonic ideals based upon
Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth.
I have endeavored to make every Master, and every Mason, aware of our
responsibility to the youth groups by providing meeting places in Masonic
Temples with fair and equitable rental charges based on understanding rather
than on financial remuneration. On December 23, 1974, I sent a letter to every
Masonic Lodge requesting a reappraisal of their policy on rentals to effect a
reduction in rental charges whenever and wherever possible.
I am pleased to report that the response was encouraging. My hope is that
every Master will continue to assist the future leaders of America in their efforts
to give us the kind of a world we each desire tomorrow.

25

LEGEND

The gavel and base, also the case, are made of redwood burl from the
Sequoia Sempervirens which grows only in California, and is the only redwood
tree which produces the burl, with its characteristic grain.
The burl, being of rather brittle nature, did not lend itself to the carving of the
stem, and for this a piece of wood, originally intended for the neck and scroll of a
violin, was used. This piece of wood was given to me, some years ago, by an
amateur violin-maker, a gamekeeper in a remote glen in the Highlands of
Scotland. Since •these Scottish violin-makers used Swiss wood almost exclusively, I believe we can assume that this wood is Swiss, which we felt would give
an International character to the Gavel, as much so as the world wide character of
Freemasonry itself.
This, then, combined with the Burl, we felt were suitable components for the
Gavel to be used by the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of California.
In searching for a form that would be special, and different from the usual
circular turned shape, the octagon was chosen. This gave us an eight-sided base
on which could be depicted scenes peculiar to California-the bear, etc.
The octagonal gold plate with the Grand Master's name, etc., was obtained
by the Most Worshipful Deputy Grand Master, Brother John F. Roberts, Jr., Past
Master of Palo Alto Lodge No. 346.
Also, noting that the redwood was rather light in weight, several cores of lead
were Introduced. This lead came from the lead window-weights of the former
Palo Alto Masonic Temple, thus giving the Gavel another Masonic connection.
These cores are concealed by the Royal Arch Penny on the bottom of the Gavel,
and the Penny also serves as a hold-fast for the extension of the stem.

125TH ANNIVERSARY CELEBRATIONS
On November 15, 1974, California Lodge No. l celebrated its 125th
Anniversary as a Masonic Lodge in California with a gala dinner-dance at the St.
Francis Yacht Club in San Francisco. The evening was enjoyed by the large
gathering of members and their ladies in attendance.
On March 20, 1975, Tehama Lodge No. 3 celebrated its 125th Anniversary
with a crab-feed at their Temple in Sacramento. This event was open to Master
Masons only and it was a wonderful evening of fellowship.
At this Anniversary Celebration the Master of Tehama Lodge No. 3 requested
the Grand Master to use their historic "Miners Bible." This Bible is more than
125 years old and has a distinguished history. It was used at the formation
meeting of the Grand Lodge of California, at the cornerstone ceremony for the
State Capital Building, at the lOlst Annual Communication (lOOth Anniversary)
of Grand Lodge of California in 1950, at the cornerstone ceremony for California
Masonic Memorial Temple here on Nob Hill in 1956 and is being used during
this 125th Anniversary Session of Grand Lodge. We are indeed grateful to have
had the privilege of adding to and extending the history of this book of Holy
Writings.
To Tehama Lodge No. 3, thank you for the honor.

I had the pleasure of presenting a third 75 Year Veteran Button on June 26,
1975, to Brother Harry Childs Corey, a member of E. F. W. Ellis Lodge No. 633
in Illinois. Brother Corey, who was 99 years old, is deaf and blind. His wife
attended the presentation ceremony along with Grand Lecturer H. Douglas
Lemons. The pin was presented in the Corey's apartment in Long Beach.

GRAND LODGE HISTORY PuBLICATION COMMITTEE
The publication to commemorate the One Hundred Twenty Fifth Year History
of the Grand Lodge of California, from 1850 to 1975, has now been completed .
It is available and will be sold during this Annual Communication at the modest
price of $8.50.
I am sure that each of you will want to purchase a copy before the close of the
Communication. It is a most interesting publication, easy to read, and will be of
great value to our members as a reference book. It consists of 288 pages printed
on high quality, coated book paper and is hardbound with gold stamping on the
cover.
Brother Edward Stansel, Chairman of the Grand Lodge History Publication
Committee, and the other members of this Committee are to be commended for
their untiring efforts to complete this history for your use and enjoyment.
PRESENTATION OF 75 YEAR PINS
On December 5, 1974, your Grand Master had the honor and privilege of
presenting a 75 Year Veteran Button to Brother Epward Verner Dales, a Past
Master of Santa Monica Lodge No. 307. He served as Master in 1904 and 1905.
Brother Dales had served as Mayor of Riverside for many years. He affiliated
with Evergreen Lodge No. 259 in Riverside where he now holds membership.
Again on April 16, 1975, your Grand Master was honored when he presented
a 75 Year Veteran Button to William Jasper Rolfe, a member of Nevada Lodge
No. 13. He resides in the city of Mentone near Redlands. Although bedridden he
was most appreciative of the presentation.

27

GRAND MASTER'S RELIEF FuND
On November 14, 1974, a check in the amount of $500.00 was forwarded to
Raul A. Caceres, Consul for Honduras and a Master Mason, payable to the
Honduras Relief Program. The Government of Honduras had estimated that
nearly 100,000 persons were left destitute and homeless as a result of Hurricane
Fifi which struck that country. A letter from Brother Caceres expressed his
heartfelt thanks for the generosity and the concern of the members of the Grand
Lodge of California.
I am grateful for the generosity of the Masons of California who have made it
possible for your Grand Master to make this contribution in their name.
CONFERENCE OF GRAND MASTERS OF NORTH AMERICA
On February 17, 1975, the Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Grand
Secretary and Past Grand Masters Eugene S. Hopp and Lester S. McElwain had
the pleasure of attending the Conference of Grand Masters in Washington D.C.
On the date designated for the observance of Washington's Birthday we
traveled to the George Washington Masonic National Memorial in Alexandria,
Virginia. The highlight of this meeting was the visit of the President of the
United States, Gerald R. Ford, who gave a beautiful and inspiring message on
Masonry. He was present for the unveiling of a bronze plaque showing him as
President, which was placed on the wall along with similar plaques for each of
the Masonic Presidents of the United States.
The Conference itself was very informative and educational. We were
grateful to have had the opportunity to attend this session.
ALL MASONIC FAMILY RECEPTION
On Sunday, February 2, 1975, the Inspectors and Lodges of Division Five
hosted a reception for the Grand Master at the Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles.
The entire program was planned by the Assistant Grand Lecturer, George W.
Perkins and the Inspectors of Division Five. Brother Perkins acted as the Master
of Ceremonies. The fullest support was given by Al Malaikah Shrine Temple and

SELECTION OF IBE JUNIOR GRAND WARDEN

At the 1974 Annual Communication legislation was approved to provide for
the appointment of a committee to recommend a member of Grand Lodge for the
office of Junior Grand Warden. Section 32 of the C.M.C. states: "The Past
Grand Masters and three members of this Grand Lodge to be appointed annually
by the Grand Master to serve for a single term only, and concurrently with the
term of the Appointing Grand Master, and who are not past or present elected
Grand Officers, shall constitute a committee to recommend to the Grand Lodge a
member thereof for selection as Junior Grand Warden."
In compliance with this legislation on November 12, 1975, I appointed the
following members of Grand Lodge to serve on this committee: Hugh J.
Cameron, Past Master of La Brea Lodge No. 650 at Los Angeles, Richard H.
Kelly, Senior Warden of Silver Gate Lodge No. 296 at San Diego, and Francis
Lewis, Past Master of Santa Barbara Lodge No. 192 at Santa Barbara. The
committee met on January 26, 1975, in Los Angeles with the Past Grand Masters
and the three members named above present. The appointed members took an
active part in the discussion at the meeting and were very helpful in selecting the
recommendee. On January 31, 1975, the name of the recommendee, with his
biographical sketch, was sent to the Grand Lodge Officers, all Committeemen,
the Inspectors and the Master of each Lodge.
Section 32, C.M.C., states that "the recommendee, alternately, shall be a
member of a Lodge in the North and of a Lodge in the South." In 1975 the
recommendee iii to be from the South. For that reason the three members of
Grand Lodge appointed to this Committee were members of Lodges in the South.
As a matter of policy it is my recommendation that this procedure be followed in
the future so that the members to be considered will be known to the committee
members.

DECISION NO. l
On April l, 1975, I was requested to make a decision regarding the physical
qualification of a prospective Candidate for the Degrees.
The man's physical problem was described as follows:
''The prospective applicant was born with a deformity/instability of the lower
right leg which necessitates him wearing an ankle brace. The instability does
not allow the man to walk without the brace which is attached to his right
shoe. The left shoe must also be worn as the built-up right shoe would
otherwise cause him to walk with one leg much longer than the other, putting
undue strain on the right leg. The physical affliction which this man suffers is
entirely corrected by the use of the brace and the wearing of the shoes .

The matter which needs a decision is really two parts. First, can and should
the metallic brace be covered in an acceptable fashion for the ritual requirement
of the First Degree and subsequent Degrees? Secondly, does or does not the
requirement that he wear both shoes in order to walk exclude him from
consideration for Degrees?"
On April 9, 1975, I sent the following letter:
"It is my decision that the applicant cannot conform to our ritual under
Annotation 512-a of the C.M.C., and his physical affliction is sufficient to
disqualify him under Annotation 512-h of the C.M.C."

of DeMolay to engage in the sale of tickets for the Shrine East-West Football

DECISION No. 3
The Grand Master was asked for a decision as to whether or not a Lodge could
expend monies from its refreshment fund for the following:
"Is it possible for a Lodge, or District, to charter one or more buses for a trip,
charging the member or his friend (wife or children) for the bus trip, a no-host
luncheon, and on the way home stop for dinner and charge the dinner expense
to the Lodge."

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

33

It was my decision that it was proper for a Lodge to expend from its
refreshment fund for this purpose under Section 412, C.M.C., provided: that
the invitation to participate in the event was extended to each member of the
Lodge; that the Lodge had approved a motion for this expenditure from its
refreshment fund at a Stated Meeting in the month preceding the month in
which the event is to be held, and with the amount of expenditure per member
specified in the motion; that the cost to the Lodge be reasonable and that the
total cost of each dinner to be paid for from the Lodge Refreshment Fund not
include any charges for alcoholic beverages (including beer or wine), and that
the expenditure was within the limits provided for in Section 412, C.M .C.
GRAND MASTER'S RECOMMENDATION No. 1

In the past several years more and more Lodges have consolidated. When two
or more Lodges do consolidate, the question has been raised as to the status of the
Master who does not continue as Master of the consolidated Lodge. Is he a Past
Master?
Annotation 490-d of the C.M.C. states that "a Master must serve to the end
of his term to be a Past Master. If he resigns during his term of office he loses that
title.'' It is my opinion that, on the effective date of consolidation of two or more
Lodges, the elected Master who does not become the Master of the Lodge thus
formed has served to the end of his term and has complied with Annotation 490-d
of the C.M.C. He is, therefore, entitled to the title of Past Master.
I, therefore, recommend that Section 490 be amended by inserting after
"jurisdiction" in the fourteenth line, "when two or more Lodges consolidate,
the Masters of the Lodge or Lodges consolidating who do not become Master of
the consolidateq Lodge become Past Masters of the consolidated Lodge thus
formed.
GRAND MASTER'S RECOMMENDATION No. 2

On November 25, 1974, it was brought to my attention by the Inspector of the
516th Masonic District that on Wednesday, November 6, 1974, at the Stated
Meeting of Canoga Lodge No. 611, the Master ordered the following action to be
taken:
1. That the elected officers of the Canoga Park Building Association be
removed from office and that all accounts and business papers be turned over to
the Secretary and Treasurer of the Lodge and;
2. That the previous dues increase voted by the Lodge, and approved by
Grand Lodge, be declared nul and void.
A Past Master of the Lodge lodged an objection to those decisions, as
provided for in Section 484 of the C.M.C., and requested the Grand Master to
consider the Master's decision.
I appointed the Senior Grand Warden, Assistant Grand Lecturer of Division
Five and the Inspector to investigate the actions of the Master and make a report
to me. On November 27, 1974, a meeting was held with the Master. The facts

which had been related to me were confirmed. The Senior Grand Warden stated

RECOMMENDATION NO. 3
On May 22, 1975, I requested the Grand Pursuivant and the Grand Tiler to
investigate the unusual circumstances surrounding the request for and the
granting of a dimit to the Senior Warden of San Dimas Lodge No. 428. An
extensive investigation was conducted and on June 9, 1975, I received a
complete written report. It revealed the following:
The investigation revealed that the Master had been informed of an alleged
offense of child molestation by the Senior Warden and that the child involved
was the step-daughter of the Senior Warden.
The Master did not try to determine whether or not there was a basis for the
charge or if it was ill-conceived and frivolous.
The Master acted improperly in directing the Secretary to issue the dimit at
the request of the Senior Warden, prior to the request being reported to the
Lodge at a Stated Meeting.
The Master, instead of requesting a dispensation by Lodge action to hold a
special election for the Office of Senior Warden, appointed the then Junior

35

The complete eight (8) page confidential report of the investigation is on
file in the Grand Secretary's Office.
As recommended in the report, concurred in by the Assistant Grand
Lecturer of Division VI, your Grand Master took the following action:
The Inspector of District No. 610 was removed from office. The Master of
San Dimas Lodge No. 428 was suspended from office. The Junior Warden
was informed that he had failed in his responsibility to file charges and was
directed by the Grand Master to immediately proceed with charges of
un-Masonic conduct against the Senior Warden, who had requested and
received a dimit. He was instructed to comply with Annotation 135c of the
California Masonic Code and to convene San Dimas Lodge so that the Lodge
could take action to request a special election to fill the Office of Senior
Warden and such other offices as may become vacant thereby. All instructions
were complied with.
It is most regrettable that this entire series of events was permitted to occur. I
recommend that the suspension of the Master of San Dimas Lodge No. 428 be
made permanent.
RECOMMENDATION NO. 4
ILLEGAL COACHING AND RAISING OF A MASON

On or about December 1, 1969, Mizpah Lodge No. 378 accepted a petition
for the Degrees of Masonry. After investigation the applicant was elected and
received his Entered Apprentice Degree on January 12, 1970. The record shows
that there was considerable difficulty in coaching the candidate for examination
in the Entered Apprentice Degree. He was finally examined on January 31, 1972,
in Mizpah Lodge and was passed to the Degree of Fellow Craft on March 20,
1972.
The Master of Mizpah Lodge No. 378 and the Secretary of Hollywood Lodge
No. 355 then verbally made unauthorized arrangements for the coaching of this

36

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Brother by Hollywood Lodge. This was a grave error when the Master failed to
request authority from the Lodge, since the Master has no authority to request
courtesy coaching by another Lodge (Annotation 548-c). The fact remains that
the candidate was coached and examined in Hollywood Lodge on February 28,
1974, and received the Master Mason Degree on the same night, all without
proper authority.
The action by Officers of Hollywood Lodge No. 355 in not obtaining from
Mizpah Lodge No. 378 written authority for coaching and conferring the Third
Degree is a serious violation of our Masonic law. On November 5, 1974, I
directed the Assistant Grand Lecturer of Division V to read a letter of reprimand
in open Lodge to the Officers and Members present at the December Stated
Meeting of Mizpah Lodge and of Hollywood Lodge. I further directed that
Mizpah Lodge take action at the December Stated Meeting to correct the error
pursuant to Section 548-a, C.M.C., which was done.
Obviously the candidate was an innocent victim of poor administration on the
part of both Lodges. I could have been much more severe, but there were
extenuating circumstances and my consideration was in the direction of leniency.
This matter was closed with peace and harmony and with the full cooperation of
Hollywood Lodge No. 355 and Mizpah Lodge No. 378.
It is my recommendation that the action of the Grand Master be approved.

RECOMMENDATION NO. 5
USE OF LODGE FuNDS FOR BICENTENNIAL COMMUNITY PROORAMS

On December 2, 1974, I was requested to make a ruling "as to whether or not
Lodge funds could be expended for a joint Bicentennial celebration with the
Bicentennial Commission of a city and a Unified School District."
A number of inquiries were made in the same general area regarding Masonic
Lodges participating in these programs.
Section 410, C.M.C. clearly states: "The expenditure of funds for any
program required by the Grand Lodge, or the Grand Master, shall be deemed to
be a part of the necessary expense of the Lodge." Since the Grand Lodge of
California has endorsed the idea of a Bicentennial celebration in 1976 for the
200th birthday of the United States of America, I consulted with the Deputy
Grand Master, who will serve as Grand Master during our Bicentennial year, and
sent the following recommendations to each Lodge in this jurisdiction:
1. Each Lodge Bicentennial Committee prepare a budget of expenditures
applying to the Lodge, regardless of whether the proposed program is a Lodge
program or a joint venture with other groups.
2. The proposed budget be carefully reviewed by the Officers and the
Inspector of the Lodge before it is presented to the Lodge for approval.
3. Unless the Bicentennial Celebration is combined with either a Public
Schools or Constitution Month Observance Program (mandatory programs of
Grand Lodge permitting use of General Funds) the expenditure should be limited
by funds available for social purposes. (See Sections 410 and 412, C.M.C.)

DEOSION (l)

The Committee on Ritual:
Your Committee on Ritual having been assigned the Grand Master's Decision
No. l, submits the following report:
We applaud the applicant for his sincerity of intention and for his desire to
partake of our degrees in his quest for a more meaningful relationship with his
fellowman. We also recognize the element of emotion that could prevail among
the members of the Lodge to which the application was directed.
We must, however, in applying the law as adopted by this Grand Lodge,
report that the applicant does not meet the requirements of sections 512-a and
512-h of the C.M.C.; neither can he substantiate conforming to what the several
degrees require of him.

judgment. Right Worshipful, I move that Decision No. l of the Grand Master be
Approved.

DECISION (2)
REGARDING MEMBERS OF THE ORDER OF DEMOLA Y
SELLING TICKETS FOR THE
SHRINE EAST-WEST FOOTBALL GAME

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
In response to a request for a decision relative to the sale of tickets for the
Shrine East-West Football Game by members of the Order of DeMolay, for
which activity that Order would receive one dollar for each ticket sold by its
members, the Grand Master decided that the activity was permissible under
Section 333-p of the C.M.C.
It is the opinion of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes that
Annotation "p" of Section 333 applies when the return is exclusively used for
charitable purposes. It does not appear that the return expected in this case
qualifies as charity.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends that this
decision be not approved, but that if the distribution of tickets by DeMolay is
now in process it may continue. However, Section 333-x should continue to be
the policy of this Grand Lodge.
Adopted.

DECISION (3)

The Grand Master has the power to suspend the Master of any Lodge from the
exercise of the powers and duties of his office, for good reason shown, until the
next Annual Communication (Section 129 C.M.C.).
It is the opinion of your Committee on Jurisprudence that the Grand Master
acted properly in suspending the Master of Canoga Lodge No. 611. The question
of whether or not such suspension is to be made permanent is a matter for the
Grand Lodge to decide. It is not a legal opinion.
By action of Grand Lodge the Grand Master's recommendation to make the
suspension permanent was
Adopted.

REGARDING EXPENDITURE OF MONIES FROM

THE LODGE'S REFRESHMENT FlJND FOR SPECIFIC DINNERS

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
This decision approved the expenditure from a Lodge's refreshment fu~d of
the cost of a dinner following a Lodge bus trip, provided there was compliance
with certain stated conditions.
The Committee considers that the decision was within the authorization
contained in Section 412, and annotation ac thereto, and complies with
annotation i to said section.
We move the approval of the decision.
Adopted.

RECOMMENDATION (1)
PAST MASTERS WHERE CONSOLIDATIONS OCCUR

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Grand Master's Recommendation Number One (1) has been referred to
the Committee on Jurisprudence and we report as follows:
This recommendation proposes to confer the status and title of Past Master on
a Master of a Lodge who does not continue as Master when two or more Lodges
consolidate.
To carry out the intent of the recommendation, we propose the following:
RESOLVED that Section 490 of the California Masonic Cbde be amended by
inserting after "jurisdiction" in line fourteen thereof the following sentence:
''When two or more Lodges consolidate, the Masters of the Lodge or Lodges
consolidating who do not become Master of the consolidated Lodge become Past
Masters of the consolidated Lodge thus formed."
To adopt this legislation at this Communication would require consideration
as an emergent matter, and we so move .
Adopted 5/6 vote (Consideration of emergent matter).
We move adoption of the legislation.
Adopted 5/6 vote.

RECOMMENDATION (2)
SUSPENSION OF MASTER FROM
DUTIES OF HIS OFFICE

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has considered the action of the Grand
Master as set forth in this recommendation.

RECOMMENDATION (3)
RELATING TO SUSPENSION OF MASTER OF
SAN DIMAS LODGE No. 428

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has considered the action of the Grand
Master as set forth in this recommendation.
The Grand Master has the power to suspend the Master of any Lodge from the
exercise of the powers and duties of his office, for good cause shown, until the
next Annual Communication (Section 129 C.M.C.). He also has the power to
remove and appoint the successors of any appointive officer (Section 132
C.M.C.). An Inspector is an appointive officer.
It is the opinion of your Committee on Jurisprudence that the Grand Master
acted properly in removing the Inspector of Masonic District No. 610 and
suspending the Master of San Dimas Lodge No. 428. The question of whether or
not such suspension of the Master is to be made permanent is a matter for Grand
Lodge to decide. It is not a legal opinion.
By action of Grand Lodge the recommendation of the Grand Master that the
suspension of the Master of San Dimas Lodge No. 428 be made permanent was
Adopted.
RECOMMENDATION (4)
ILLEGAL COACHING AND RAISING OF A MASON

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has considered the action of the Grand
Master as set forth in this recommendation.
It is a duty of the Grand Master to exercise a general and careful supervision
over the craft, and see that the Constitution and Regulations of the Grand Lodge
are strictly maintained, supported, and obeyed (Section 142 C.M.C.).
It is the opinion of your Committee on Jurisprudence that the Grand Master
acted properly in handling this matter.
We move the approval of the action of the Grand Master.
Adopted.

PROCLAMATION
YOUTH ACTIVITIES WEEK

The Fifty-fifth Anniversary of the founding of a Public Schools
Observance by the Grand Lodge Free and Accepted Masons of California again
focuses our attention on the vital need for the Masons of this jurisdiction
to support our state system of public education.
The future strength of America lies in its public schools and the
dedic·ated men and women who have the responsibility for educating our American youth -- the leaders of tomorrow.
we should be constantly aware of the continuou~ e~forts of legisla~
tive and organizational attempts to trespass on the pri~ciples of our public
educational system. A system designed to furnish the high7s~ degree of education to every American, regardless of race, creed or religi~n: A system
designed to be completely devoid of partisan influence or religious dogmas.
I, therefore, proclaim the month of April 1975, as Public Schools
Month and the theme selected for this annual Observance will be
"Public Schools - Freedom's First Frontier".
I further direct that:
All Constituent Lodges in California and Hawaii actively
participate in an appropriate Public Schools Program.
The suggestions offered by the Public Schools Committee
be followed wherever possible.
No Lodge meetings be held during this month for purposes
other than the local observation of Public Schools Month
with the exception of Stated Meetings.

This Proclamation be read at the March and April Stated
Meetings of every Lodge.

PROCLAMATION
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH

At the Constitutional Convention of 1767, held nearly 200
years ago, a document unique in the history of mankind was engrossed
on parchment. There were thirty-nine signers of our Constitution and
twenty-three were Freemasons. Since that time the fabric of our
Nation has been woven with the golden threads of Masonry always
evident, creating a tapestry that has been the centerpiece of admiration by people of all nations.
The basic principles of Freemason~y and the basic principles
of our Constitution are inseparable. The members of our Fraternity
played an important part in the creation of the United States of
America.
Today, more than any other time in our history, the Masons
of California should be vitally concerned with conditions that exist
in our Nation. Certain elements are actively engaged in an attempt
to destroy our Constitution and our form of government.
Each of us,
as Masons and as Americans, must be constantly vigilant to fight for
and protect the freedoms granted to us by our forefathers.
I, therefore, designate the month of September 1975 as
Constitution observance Month and direct every Lodge in this Jurisdiction to actively engage in a meaningful patriotic program during
the month.
Each program should be well-planned in advance and encourage public attendance and participation.
I further direct that this Proclamation b e read at the
August and September Stated Meetings and, wherever possible, be reprinted in Lodge bulletins for September 1975.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
In accordance with requirements of our Masonic law, I am pleased to submit
herewith my fifteenth Annual Report of the year's recorded business of the Grand
Lodge and related duties. All financial records for the Grand Lodge , the Masonic
Homes of California, the California Masonic Foundation, the California Masonic
Retirement Plan and the California Masonic Memorial Temple have been audited
by Hurdman and Cranstoun. Supporting papers, vouchers and books are on file
in the Grand Lodge Office.
As required by law, the Chairman and members of the Committee on Finance
have reviewed details of disbursements made by Grand Lodge during the year.
The recording of all monies received and credited to the accounts under his
name and custody are reflected in the Grand Treasurer's report.
The Office Staff continues to serve the various Grand Lodge entities with
appreciation and enthusiasm.

ACCOUNTING R ECORDS

Since the installatio n of a small computer in our Accounting Office, this year
we have continued to bring work previously handled through accounting services
companies on a fee ha sis. into the Grand Lodge Office. For the first time, Annual
Re turn state ments for Lodges were prepared entirely within this office and
economies resulted . Certain adjustments also were made in the Homes accounting records to accomodate cost control programs recently expanded a! o ur H? mes
and to make comprehensive, periodic financial statements more readily ava il able
to Homes Trustees. We have on order a line-printe r to help speed up the process
of accounting mechanic~ which w ill permit additiona l accounting records to be
handled by our staff.

Prese ntation of Veteran Buttons continues to reflect the enormou s increase in
the membership of the jurisdktion fo llo wing World War I. We antici pate a
gradual decli ne in presentations after the next se veral years. For the period
between September 1, 1974, and September l , 1975. a to tal of l , 496 veteran
members received Fifty Year Butto ns and Certificates. This number is s uhstan tially below the peak year of 1970, when we presented 1. 912 Veteran Buttons .
From the beginning of the program to the present 23,3 14 Brothers have
received this coveted award . During this same period fifteen Seventy-Five Year
Buttons have been presented to California members.

T HE H EARTBEAT OF MASONRY

The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California has urged the
Office Staff tu develop an overall plan of fund raising for our Masonic charities .
The intent of suc h a program is to coordi nate M asonic charitable giving and to
expand a nd su ppleme nt the present efficie nt organization of th e Masonic Home s
Endowment Board.
There is a real need for expansion of the activitie s of the California Mason ic
Foundation and for the development of the much needed Library and Museu m in
connection with the Califronia Masonic Memorial Temple . Studies have been
authorized and conducted for this latter project. To meet the needs of the
rehabilitation costs for the Home at Union City, to expand the operation of the
California Masonic Foundation and to add the cultural cen ter to the California
Masonic Memorial Temple are all worthy projects. They can be developed
without detracting from the continued success of fund raising for any one of the
programs.
A spec ial Committee has been appointed cons isting of our Senior Grand
Warden Kermit A. Jacobson, o ur Junior Grand Warden Do nald B . McCaw, the
Grand Orator Donald Ingalls and your Grand Secretary. With the assistance of
Brother Varnum Paul, legal counsel, work is under way to develop new
brochures appealing particularly to those persons interested in updating their

66

PROCEEDlNGS OF THE

wills or in making life income gifts to a project of their own choice . We have,
under the Tax Refonn Act of 1969, qualified to extend such a life income gift to
all interested parties. A new brochure entitled "The Heartbeat of Masonry" will
be ready for distribution in the not too distant future.
Question: What is a life income gift?
Answer: It is a gift made during one's lifetime. A life income gift to the
Masonic Homes of California is primarily motivated by the desire to support the
less fortunate, yet it has the secondary advantage of benefitting the donor through
the use of the charitable tax deduction laws.
Life income giving adds immeasurably to stability and enables the Trustees to
plan for the future. Such gifts will ultimately provide unreslricted funds to meet a
host of critical needs.
Also, we will have a special brochure which will describe the functioning of
the "Pooled Income Fund" already qualified under Internal Revenue Regulations. For the present, our first efforts are being directed toward the Masonic
Homes of California in order to complete the program of rehabilitation at Union

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
The Committee on By -Laws:
With five of its seven Members present Saturday Morning. October 11, 1975,
your Committee on By-Laws began its review of the matters referred to it.
Your Committee checked and re-checked 124 By-Law changes made by the
Constituent Lodges.
All of the By-Law amendments and resolutions were found to be in order.
Ex hibit "A " of the Grand Secretary's report. to which the Members may
refer sets forth the changes . Noticeable in By- Law changes this year were 78
Lodges increasing dues, and 12 Lodges increasing the fee. Nine changes in
meeting place causes us to believe that Lodges are still building new Temples .

73

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

As in the past your Committee suggests that all Lodges review Article X of
their By-Laws which sets forth the maximum authority of the Charity Committee
of the Lodge, during the interval between Stated Meetings .
Your Committee would like to point out that the Charity provision is a very
important part of your By- Laws, and could cause embarrassment to your Lodge,
if the present amount allowable is small. The old $25.00 standard by which so
many Lodges operated a few years ago may not be any charit y at all.
Even though all of the amendments reviewed were approved, your Committee
found that the matter of designating Holidays in the By-Laws remains troublesome. Article Ill of the Uniform Code of By-Laws, which permits exceptions to
the regular date of the Stated Meetings of a Lodge. limits the exception to legal
Holidays and during the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge .
With regard to the legal Holidays, these should be specifically named, so that
there will be no mi sunderstanding as to whether a particular day is or is not a
Holiday. Further, the particular Legal Holiday should be identified by NAME
AND NOT BY DATE; that is New Year's Day is preferable to January 1st, and
Independence Day is preferable to July 4th, because such description leaves no
doubt that the exception applies when these days are celebrated on Monday in a
year when these dates fall on a Sunday.
Particular attention :-.houkl be paid to this point of designation of Ho lidays and
especially the Monday night Lodges . By action of Congress, several Holidays
will be celebrated on Monday even though they actually fall on another day of the
week.
When making a By-Law change. the Lodges should contact the Grand
Secretary's Office for the proper forms. Also a Lodge s hould provide for an
alternate date in case a Stated Meeting falls during the Annual Communication of
Grand Lodge. While only those Lodges whose Stated Meetings are during the
second week of the month are affected, the date of any Annual Communication
may be changed for any year. So the contingency should be provided for.
In reviewing the resolutions having to do with the change of Meeting place by
various Lodges, your Committee found that in se veral cases a Lodge moved to a
new Meeting place without following the formal procedures as set forth in the
California Masonic Code. The procedure for the changing of a Meeting place is
set fonh in California Masonic Code, Section 372.
We would like to impress upon all of the Officers in attendance today , that
they should check the Masonic Code and By-Laws of their respective Lodges
before making any changes in Meeting place. Dues, Charit y Fund, and the times
of Meetings.
We wish to comme nd the Officers of the Lodges who so carefully followed
our Masonic Code .
This Committee co ncurs with that portion of the GranJ Secretary's report
referred to it by the Committee on Distribution.
This Committee wishes to thank the Grand Secretary and his staff for their
efficiency and diligence in guiding those who needed assistance in properly
adopting the changes. and for the guidance of thi s Committee .

Most Worshipful, we ask that Grand Lodge approve the amendments and
resolutions listed in Exhibit .. A., of the Grand Secretary's report with the
additions herein above specified , and that the repon of the Committee on
By-Laws be received.

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
The Committee on Grievances:
There have been referred to your Committee on Grievances since the 1974
Communication, twenty-six trial records. of which four are petitions for
restoration .
In Trial Records Nos. 2042. 2046, 2047, 2048 , 2049, 2050, 2051 , 2052 ,
2053, 2054, 2055, 2057, 2058, 2059, 2060. 2063, 2064, and 2065, your
Committee has reviewed each record and finds that the proper procedure was
followed in each case; that the results are supported by the evidence in the
respective records; and there was substantial compliance with the procedural
requirements of our Constitution and Ordinances; and that there were no
miscarriages of justice. We therefore offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED. that in each of the above numbered Trial Records judgment of
the Trial Commission or the Trial Master and the penalty imposed be and the
same are ratified , reaffim1ed and approved.
The Petition for Restoration in Trial Record No. 1525 from Barstow Lo dge
No. 682 has carefully been considered , and the showing made by the applic ant
leads us to believe that such applicant is worthy to be restored to the rights and
privileges of Masonry and has substantially complied with the requirements of
Grand Lodge for restoration. We therefore offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the petition for restoration in Trial Record No. 1525 be
granted .
Your Committee has carefully examined the Petitions for Restoration in Trial
Record No. 1944, Alexandria Lodge No. 53 l (now Educator No . 554) and Trial
Record No. 1971, El Cajon Valley Lodge No. 576 and found that in each case
the crime committee was extremely contrary to the tenets of Masonry and that
there has been an insufficient showing of rehabilitation . We therefore offer the
following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the Petition for Restoration in Trial Record No. 1944 and
Trial Record No. 1971 be denied.

75

This is a petition for restoration. The accused was convicted in 1965 of
inducing his candidates' coach to reduce the lecture of the Entered Apprent ice
Degree to typewritten form to assist him in passing the required examination. At
the time, both were members of Loyalty Lodge No. 579.
The facts were not known until after the accused became a Master Mason but.
upon disclosure, both members were tried, found guilty and suspended in 1965.
The candidates' coach was re-admitted to membership shortly thereafter.
The accused petitioned Loyalty Lodge for restoration in 1967 and was turned
down . He petitioned Grand Lodge in 1969 and was also denied re-admission .
Loyalty Lodge re-admitted the candidates ' coach based on his sincere
expressions of remorse and contrition. It has, however, clearly indicated its
desire that the accused not be a member of that Lodge again. There are , however.
a number of letters in the file from members of other Lodge s indicating a strong
belief in the accused's rehabilitation and expressing a desire that he become a
member of their Lodges .
While a maj ority of the members of Loyalty Lodge have not been convinced
of the sincerity of the accused's statements of remorse, a number of the members
have been and they rely in part on a number of very forceful and compelling pleas
by the accused that he be allowed to once again enjoy the rights of Masonry .
In light of Loyalty Lodge's restoration of the candidates' coach, your
Committee unanimously felt that the accused should be restored, thereby making
him a Mason-at-large with the right to petition another Lodge for membership.
Your Committee offers the following Resolution:
RESOLVED . that the petition of the accused in Trial No. 1870 for restoration
to the rights and. privileges of Masonry be granted.
TRIAL RECORD NO. 2056
A member of Covina Lodge 334 was charged with falsely and fraudulently
answering Questions No . 12 and 16 of his application for degrees in that he had
been convicted of extortion, escape from a penal institution and violation of
parole in the year 1960 at the age of 19, some 14 years before he made
application for the degrees .
The extortion consisted of he and a number of others while in the Marine
Corps representing to boot marines that they were M. P. s and confiscating their
alcoholic beverages. He was sentenced, placed in jail, and escaped. He was
caught and incarcerated for 28 months. After being discharged. his conduct
thereafter was commendable, receiving a certificate of rehabilitation and an
excellent report from his probation officer and has since led an exemplary life.
Your Committee has always felt that misstatement in an application as to a
prior criminal record should always be grounds for expulsion. The Trial
Commission in this case by a vote of 5 to 3 agreed .
Regretfully , however, we must recommend a retrial of this case due to serious
questions regarding the actual impaneling of the Trial Commission, the conduct

PROCEEDrNGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of members of the Commission during the trial and the deliberations of the
Commission as reported to your Committee by the capable Trial Master and a
troubled member of the Commission.
While we do not wish to criticize members of a Masonic Lodge for being
over-zealous in the defense of our institution, we feel we must insist that a
Brother Mason, while he is still such, must be accorded that degree of fairness
and impartiality as may be required of one Brother to another always bearing in
mind that "justice is that standard or boundary of right which enables us to
render every man his just dues," no less a Brother Master Mason.
Because we are not convinced that such has been the case here, the matter
should be reversed and sent back to the Lodge for retrial with the suggestion that
the incoming Grand Master consider the retrial being held in another Lodge.
We therefore submit the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the decision of the Trial Commission be set aside and that
Trial Record 2056 be returned for retrial with the recommendation that the
incoming Grand Master refer this trial record to another Lodge for such retrial.
