TRIAL RECORD No. 2061

The Trial Master in this case ruled that the response of the accused to the
charges against him constituted a plea of guilty to specification number one. That
specification charged that the accused drew two checks for his own use on the
account of the Masonic Temple Association of which he was Treasurer, one
check payable to himself in the amount of $672.00 and one check payable to
himself in the amount of $436.37. The checks were unauthorized and were not
accounted for in the Temple Association records. The bank paid the checks.
After investigation, the Trial Master found the accused guilty of specification
number one and fixed the penalty at suspension.
The ruling that the response of the accuse.d constituted a plea of guilty and the
procedure appear to be proper. However, although the accused made restitution,
it was after denial and equivocation on his part. Also, the fact that the accused
was acting in a fiduciary capacity, which re.quires the highest degree of good
faith . and the fact that the offenses were committed against his Brethren both
require a stronger sanction.
RESOLVED , that the finding of guilty in Trial Record No. 2061 be
approved. but that the penalty be raised to expulsion and the member expelled
from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
TRIAL RECORD No. 2062

This matter, contrary to most matters before your Committee, is not a trial
review. There has been no trial. The issue before the Committee is whether a trial
is necessary under our law.
The accused. a Master Mason in good standing, was a dual member of A. F.
E. Irwin Lodge No. 645 in California and Grahamville Lodge No. 707 in
Kentucky.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2066

The Acc used, a member of Long Beac h Lodge No. 327, was charged in the
Los Ange les County Municipal Court with three felony counts of receiving stolen
property. He was charged with having purchased: a .357 Luger Pi stol and
Holster; a Winchester Rifle; and some stereo equipment. all of which he knew to
be stole n. On November 19. 1974 , he plead guilty in Los Angeles Supe rior Court
of one count of receiving stole n property, to-wit, the purchase of the . 357 L ugar
Pistol. On January 10, 1975 , the accu sed was sentenced to pay a fine of
$1,000.00, six months suspe nded term in County jail and three years probation, a
misdemeanor sentence.
Charges of un-Masonic conduct were filed against the accused allegi ng one
specification, of receiving stolen property, a crime. He was tried by Long Beac h
Lodge No. 327 and found not guilty by that Lodge.
Your Grievances Committee has carefully e xamined the transcript of the
Trial. some 36 pages in length. The record indicates that the accused admitted
that he had knowledge that the weapon he purchased had been sto le n at t he
time o f the purchase. and. therefore , had knowledge of the offense he was
committing.
The record clearly indicates guilt to your Grievances Committee and we can
only feel that irregularities in the Tria l proceedings caused a miscarriage of
j ustice. Your Grievances Committee unanimously determined that it was clear
from the admissions of the accused that he had committed the offense c harged
and that the finding of Not Guilty by the Commiss ion was incorrect.
Your Grievances Committee, therefore, feels that the Commission's fi nding
of Not Guilty should be set aside and the penalty set at suspension, t hereby
reserving to the Lodge the question of his restoration.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
In just a little less than three days from now, the 1974-75 Grand Lodge year
will become the l 25th page in the history of the Grand Lodge of California.
It has been my pleasure to serve as your Grand Lecturer for the past twelve
months, and it is now my duty to render a full and detailed account of my
services during the year, setting forth therein, a report of the condition of the
Lodges within this Grand Jurisdiction .
In order to assure that all areas are accurately reported upon, this report shall
be divided into five major portions-Ritual, Inspectors, Condition of Lodges,
Hawaiian Masonry and Budget.
In working with the Ritual it has been most rewarding for me to observe the
concentration of effort which is applied at all levels of the California Ritual
Instructional system: From the Grand Lecturer and the Assistant Grand Lecturers
to the Inspectors, Coaches, Masters, Wardens and Brethren . At every station
there seems to be a fierce pride in establishing and maintaining extremely high
levels of ritual proficiency. Literally thousands of hours are spent studying,
perfecting and teaching the Ritual. . . . The Ritual Committee has met on several
occasions this year for the purpose of discussing the Ritual, Lodge Administration, and Masonic leadership, and the Assistant Grand Lecturers have held
Division Schools of instruction for the Inspectors, usually every other month
during the year. In addition to this, the Inspectors have held District Officers
Schools within their individual Districts averaging eight schools per year, and
many many individual schools of instruction have been held by the Masters and
Officers Coaches of the several Lodges within the California Jurisdiction.
According to the Inspectors' reports, these have averaged two schools on each
degree, plus one school on Masonic Law and Custom in each lodge. There have
also been thousands of private, or individual Ritual Coaching sessions at which
the Officers Coaches have tutored Lodge officers, and many dedicated Masons
have constantly studied the California Ritual, striving for no less than perfection
in the Esoteric, as well as the Monitorial work.
In the early part of this year, the Inspectors Spring Conferences were held in
each of the Six Divisions for the purpose of having the Ritual Committee and
Inspectors review all the work in a week-end long session.
The first was in Division Six at Long Beach in February, conducted by
Assistant Grand Lecturer, Ernest M. Newton.
Second was in Division Three at Los Gatos in March, conducted by Assistant
Grand Lecturer, Ulysess G. Patropulos.
Third was in Division One at Santa Rosa in April, conducted by Assistant
Grand Lecturer, Burton 0. Young.
Fourth was in Division Five at Los Angeles in May, conducted by Assistant
Grand Lecturer, George Perkins.

92

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Fifth was Division Four at Visalia in early June, conducted by Assistant
Grand Lecturer, Vernon 0. Gordon.

CONDITION OF LODGES .

Sixth was in Division Two at Sacramento in late June, conducted by Assistant
Grand Lecturer, Edward Seagle.
Attending these spring conference sessions, in addition to the Inspectors and
Ritual Committee, were the Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, the Senior and
Junior Grand Wardens and the Grand Secretary.
The great value of the Spring Conference is the opportunity which it affords
each Inspector to participate in, and comment upon, the Ritual, all under the
watchful eye of the entire Ritual Committee.
In observing the work of the Inspectors at these conferences, I can report that
the California Ritual is indeed being properly and uniformly exemplified
throughout the Jurisdiction. I personally commend the Assistand Grand Lecturers
and each of the Inspectors for their efforts in studying and teaching the California
Ritual in such a proficient manner . . . I am extremely proud of them all!!
INSPECTORS

In each of the other Jurisdictions which I have visited as your Grand Lecturer
I have inevitably been asked, "Brother Lemons, to what do you attribute the
success of California Masonry in developing and maintaining such an efficient system of Ritual and Protocol?" My answer is always in one word:
"Inspectors."
Now there is certainly nothing magical or mystical about Inspectors. . . . A
lot of Jurisdictions have them ... It's just that here in California, we have a
group of Inspectors who are a cut above the average, and neither is that by
accident. There are several very important pre-requisites to the office of Inspector, the most important of which is, Leadership ability. Also high on the list
of pre-requisites are such things as tolerance, and the ability to deal with people
in a friendly and understanding manner. The California Masonic Inspector is
constantly guided by the words of the Second Degree charge: "To judge with
candor, admonish with friendship, and reprehend with justice."
Supported by such worthy principles, our California Masonic Inspector
demonstrates a natural ability to aid and assist, rather than guide and direct.
Twenty-six of our Inspectors have this year retired from service in the
lnspectoral Corps, thereby giving an equal number of eager new Brothers the
opportunity to serve Masonry in this very important assignment. To those of our
old and valued friends who have seen fit to step aside, we offer our sincere
gratitude for the loyalty they have demonstrated to Masonry and to the Corps .
We wish them God Speed in new assignments, or peace and happiness in
retirement. These Brothers will be forever held in high esteem by a grateful
Fraternity. To those many new Brothers who are assuming the duties of Inspector
this year, we welcome you to service in the finest Inspectoral Corps in the World.
We look forward to serving with you, and we pledge you our complete support in
all your lawful undertakings.

93

!urning ~o~ to the main part of this report, I sincerely wish I could say that
all is well withm the Lodges of the California Jurisdiction: Such however is not
the case. ~onditions within the Lo~ges are certainly not what they should be.
Report~ng to the Grand Lodge m years gone by, I have warned of potential
problems m the areas of Lodge Administration, membership participation and
replacement of Lodge Officers, but let me give it to you officially: Nearly eighty
percent of the Inspectors report this year that they feel problems within our
Lodges are three-fold: Number one is declining interest on the part of Lodge
membership. Number two is reluctance of Brothers to serve as Lodge Officers
and three is the lack of Candidates for the degrees. I do not disagree with this
~ssessment. I do most vehemently disagree that any of these problems are
mso~uable! They are only temporary manifestations, and their solution requires
nothing more than some good old fashioned Masonic Leadership!!
Now let's just talk about that for a moment.
In the first place, Masons DO NOT lose interest in Masonry!
Simple logic tells us this is true, for why in the name of good common sense
would any person continue to pay dues for something in which he has no
interest? . . . I repeat: Masons DO NOT lose interest in Masonry: If our
members have lost interest in attending our meetings, then it should be clear to us
~hat we are just not conducting those meetings in a manner which attracts their
mterest . . . This should be an indication to the true Masonic Leader that patterns
must be changed, and new methods found of conducting Masonic business in a
m~nner which will attract the interest of the members ... It can be; it must be; it
will be done! We must leave no stone unturned in our search for new ideas and
methods of c~ing out the mission of Masonry, but we've got to do it NOW!!
As to new Officer material, I have the following comment:
It seems that we are unable to discard the antiquated theory that if a Brother is
appointed ~unior Steward o_f the Lodge, he MUST spend the following eight
years workmg through the hne and become the Worshipful Master in the Ninth
... Well, Bre~hren, it just isn't working out that way! The type of individual we
sh~uld be seeking to serve as Master of our Lodges is a busy man, a man who is
gomg places and doing things in his Community, but certainly NOT a man who
has eight years to give waiting in line to become Master of a Masonic
Lodge: . . . . . Neit~er i.s the theory sound that says a brother MUST go through
all the chairs m the hne m order to be properly qualified to serve as Master . . .
The Brother we are talking about could very well enter the line at the station of
Junior Warden if need be, and still be eminently qualified two years later to serve
as Worshipful Master.
~s t? the appointive stations, you may rest assured that in nearly every
Cahfo~ta Lodge there are several Brothers who would welcome the opportunity
of se~mg the Lodge as an Officer for one or two years, but who would under no
condit10ns accept the responsibility of leading the Lodge. Please think about this
my Brothers, and discuss it in your Lodge. There just might be a greater store of
Officer material available to your Lodge than you have imagined.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

As regards the lack of new Candidates in our Lodges, this problem also has its
solution ... As a matter of fact, many of our Lodges have already discovered
the solution and have put it into practice.
.
The simple fact is that quite unintentionally, Masonry is projecting an
unfriendly image . . . There are many good men who would like to join the
Masonic Fraternity, but who have not done so because of the atmosphere of
secrecy with which we have surrounded ourselves ... We must remove that
image: We need to talk about Masonry; we need to welcome those individuals
who have indicated a desire to join us, and we need to tell the whole world just
what we stand for!!
It has been my pleasure to appear as guest speaker for several Layman's night
programs this year, and as a direct result of these informative sessions, over fifty
good men have petitioned for the degrees of Masonry.
The most recent such meeting was held in Searchlight Lodge No. 567 in June
of this year. This meeting was attended by nearly 200 Masons, together with
several interested non-Masons who came to hear what Masonry is all about.
Following the address and a question and answer period, 21 of those
non-Masons presented their petitions for the degrees. I congratulate Worshipful
Willis Brewer, Master of Searchlight Lodge, together with the other Masters who
have instituted the layman's night concept of Masonic education, and I commend
this program to the many other Masters who are concerned with lack of new
Candidates.
Returning from Japan last month I stopped over in Honolulu for a brief rest.
While there I was invited to attend a Masonic Dinner and dance at the officers
club of Tripler Army Hospital where I met 80 happy Masons from Educator
Lodge No. 554 of San Francisco. These Brothers had flown to Honolulu to
confer the third Degree upon Brother John J. Morris, now the newest member of
Educator Lodge. This event was a visitation between Honolulu Lodge No. 409
and Educator Lodge. Believe me Brethren, the members of these two Lodges
hav~ not lost interest in Masonry, nor will they so long as they are guided by such
excellent leaders as Worshipful Louis Schaich, Master of Educator Lodge, and
Worshipful Emerick K. Ishikawa, Master of Honolulu Lodge No. 409. I
congratulate both these Masters and the members of their Lodges for this
activity.
I was also pleased to note the activity of Menorah Lodge of Los Angeles on
Saturday evening, October 4th. This Lodge held its 50th Anniversary celebration
at the Hollywood Palladium and they had a tum away crowd of 1200 members
who saw fit to pay $25.00 per plate to participate in this celebration.
Even though I was not present, I understand that the evening was greatly
enjoyed by all, and they almost had to bum the Palladium to get people to go
home. Have the Brethren of Menorah Lodge No. 623 lost interest? I think
not. ... My congratulations also to Worshipful Albert L. Marks, Master of
Menorah, and to those 1200 Los Angeles Masons who are really enjoying their
Masonry.
Now I know there are many other Lodges and Masters who have had very
successful programs this year, and they are all to be commended for their

innovative leadership in guiding their Lodges to new activities. To those who
have been in the same old rut all year I would recommend that some thought be
given to instituting some new programs of Lodge activity to encourage membership participation. Your Ritual Committee and the Inspectors all have some new
ideas and suggestions which they will be happy to share. Much study has been
devoted to this problem this year.
In March this year, the Ritual Committee inaugurated their program of
Masonic Leadership with a Divisional Seminar in San Jose. 450 Masters,
Wardens, Inspectors, Officers and Brethren crowded into the new San Jose
Temple for this meeting. The morning session was devoted to Ritual instruction,
and the afternoon was spent listening to several excellent papers on Masonic
leadership delivered by the Assistant Grand Lecturers. The final paper on
Podium presence, or public speaking, was delivered by the Grand Orator,
Worshipful Donald Ingalls.
The second such Seminar was held in May at Santa Ana for Division Six.
When reservations passed 1100, the meeting had to be moved to the Santa Ana
Union High School Auditorium to accomodate the crowd, and this meeting was
even more successful than was the first. The talk on public speaking was
delivered by the Grand Chaplain, the Very Reverend Roland R. Bach. The most
recent leadership seminar was held on the stage of the Los Angeles Scottish Rite
Cathedral, and attendance ran somewhere over 800. These Seminars have been
very well received by the Brethren who have been more than gracious in writing
the Grand Lecturer to express their opinions, and also offer some very welcome
suggestions. It is interesting to note that the only criticism of this program voiced
by the Brethren is, "Why Haven't you done this before now, and why can't we
have the same type Seminars on a monthly basis."
As a result of these comments and our own evaluation, it is the intention of
the Ritual Committee to continue this type of leadership training throughout. the
California Jurisdiction. This decision has the unqualified support of the present
Grand Master, the incoming Grand Master and the Elective Grand Lodge Line.
November 22nd has been chosen as the date for the next leadership seminar
which will be held in the Oakland Scottish Rite Temple.

HAWAIIAN MASONRY

In late February we journeyed to Hawaii for meetings with the Inspectors,
Officers and Brethren of the Ten Hawaiian Lodges. While there, we conducted
all day schools of Ritual on Saturday and Sunday in Honolulu, and evening
schools in the Lodges of the outer islands of Hawaii, Maui and Kauai. By virtue
of their close proximity, one to the other, the seven Lodges on the island of Oahu
seem to experience far less difficulty than their sister Lodges in the Outer Islands
so far as obtaining new Officers, participating in Schools of instruction for
Officers, and carrying out the various assilmments of Masonrv.
Ritual Proficiency continues to improve in these Lodges and the all day
schools serve a most useful purpose in correcting minor discrepancies which
seem to creep into the work from time to time.

97

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The outer island Lodges continue to experience difficulty in obtaining new
Officers each year. Schools of instruction for Officers are poorly attended due to
the great distances which some of these officers must travel to attend Lodge. This
in tum reflects upon Ritual Proficiency, and the yearly visits of the Ritual
Committee to these Lodges in Hilo, Maui and Kauai are greatly beneficial in
maintaining Ritual Proficiency. The two island inspectors, Bill McKee and Ozzie
Lau are doing a tremendous job in teaching the Ritual, assisting the Masters and
Lodges in administration and activities, and serving as chief liason Officers from
the Grand Lodge. They are involved at every level of Masonic activity in Hawaii,
and they have become extremely expert in dealing with the manifold problems of
Hawaiian Masonry. They are honorable men and good Masons who give freely
of their time and talents in the service of Masonry. We salute them for their
activities.
I am extremely grateful for my association with all the wonderful Masons of
Hawaii. Their every action seems to give new meaning to the words Brotherly
Love: The word they use is "Aloha," and they not only say it, they mean it as
well. To all these wonderful Masons of Hawaii, our thanks for their many
courtesies.

Our Grand Master, a man of many talents: A singer of some note, (even
though we haven't discovered which one), a man who has spread friendship
throughout the Grand Jurisdiction this year and who has done much to further
understanding among all the Masons of California, but more than that, a good
friend to this Grand Lecturer and to all Masons.
And to you, my Brethren, I thank you one and all for the opportunity you
have given me to serve as your Grand Lecturer this year. I have enjoyed meeting
and working with each of you, and it is my sincere hope that my actions thus far
will receive your approbation.

1975-76 BUDGET

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE

96

The Ritual Committee is extremely proud of the fact that we completed the
year 1974-75 $3,000 under budget. This was due strictly to the efforts of the
Assistant Grand Lecturers and the Inspectors in keeping expense at the lowest
level possible. Consistant with this effort for 1974-75, we plan to tighten our
belts even more in the coming year in an effort to deal with projected higher
costs. Accordingly, we have submitted a budget to the Finance Committee
asking the amount of $49,000 for the year 1975-76. This figure is actually
$2,000 under the amount we requested for last year and represents the minimum
amount which we feel is necessary to teach the Ritual in the coming year.

Referred to Committee on Distribution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
That portion of the report of the Grand Lecturer relating to new programs to
encourage membership participation has been referred to the Committee on
Policy and General Purposes. At the Annual Communication in 1974, Grand
Master Ebbage recommended "the establishment and maintenance of a supervised educationru program to develop the capacities necessary for the overall
governing of Lodge affairs." He suggested that this might be administered by a
Special Committee. His recommendation was adopted. The incumbent Grand
Master, M. ·. W. · .Burton Meyer, Jr., requested the Ritual Committee to carry
out this adopted recommendation, and the report of the Grand Lecturer testifies
to their service in this regard.
It is the considered opinion of your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes that a special committee should be appointed to carry on and further
implement this important endeavor, of which the encouragement of membership
participation is obviously an integral part. The duties of the Ritual Committee are
clearly defined in the C.M.C. and the members of that committee must devote a
great amount of time, as well as specialized skill, to their duties. This Grand
Lodge has many able, experienced and willing members who can devote their
talents and their time to the development of the program recommended by Grand
Master Ebbage, and it is the judgment of the Committee on Policy and General
~urposes that this is the course that should be persued at the earliest practical
time.
Adopted.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

OPERATION OF THE HOMES
All California Masons are aware that our new Home for Children at Covina is
complete with its ten buildings for family residential Jiving. The new administration building, library, infirmary, kitchen, dining room, living room and landscaping instills pride in all Masonry to know that they truly "care for their own."
Notwithstanding the fact that the Children's Home has been built Jess than
two years, safety codes are constantly being revised and are being made
applicable to existing facilities as well as to new construction. Consequently, we
must be continually vigilant to make certain that we are not deficient. Mark E.
Schrock, Grand Pursuivant, is expert in this area and he has been of great help in
inspecting both of our Homes to insure compliance.
As was also reported at the 1974 Annual Communication in an oral supplement to the written report of the Board of Trustees, the California Department of
Social Welfare made an intensive investigation of every facit of the Skilled
Nursing Facility of our Decoto Home and found us wanting in several respects.
All corrections in the physical plant, procedures, equipment and staffing indicated in the State report have been made and we continue in good standing with
the licensing authorities.
To insure that our Decoto Home not only complied with the Jaw, but that it
provided excellent care for its residents whether or not required by law, the
California Medical Association was retained by the Board to undertake a
thorough study of our entire operation. The Committee of the Association
rendered its written report and its further recommendations have either been
implemented or are under study.
REHABILITA TION AT DECOTO

Committees of the Board are charged with specific functions such as constantly reviewing the budget and requests for capital . or other purchases, real
estate servicing and sale, insurance review, scholarship awards, maintenance and
repair at Covina, and the like. Each of these duties take countless hours each
month in addition to the study of applications for admission and outside relief,
operational material submitted by management, etc.; however, due to the
yeoman service of our Decoto Rehabilitation Committee which is chaired by
Trustee Charles Sedam, the Vice-President of the Pacific Gas and Electric
Company in charge of construction, it has been singled out for special attention
in this report.
It has been regularly reported to the Craft that major maintenance had been
deferred at Decoto pending the completion of the Covina facility which consumed the greater efforts of the Board.
Trustee Sedam is expertly assisted by Trustee "Bus" Orear, the President of
Ira W. Coburn, Inc., Builders, and Trustee Ray Howe, the Business Manager of
the Palo Alto Clinic. This Committee holds regular monthly meetings at Decoto
with representatives from management, the Secretary's office, the President and
consultants in various disciplines. In addition, special meetings are conducted
with the architect, engineers, contractors and other advisors with the goal of

101

closing the gap created by the extended period while maintenance was being
deferred.
The particulars of the improvements in the safety and comfort of our Decoto
Home by Trustees Sedam and Orear and in equipment purchase and replacement
by Trustee Howe were detailed in the Autumn 1975 issue of the California
Freemason and your attention is directed to that outstanding Masonic publication
edited by Trustee Ralph Head.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Any Mason in this jurisdiction who has never visited our Homes is earnestly
urged to do so. You will find that you will be cordially welcomed and personally
escorted on a tour of each facility.
The complete financial statement of the Masonic Homes of California and the
opinion of its auditors will be found in the published proceedings. You are
reminded, however, when reviewing those reports that, although there is a large
sum invested in our Endowment Fund, like any such fund, only its income (and
not its principal) may be expended for the operation, maintenance, rehabilitation
and replacements for the Homes.
As the income thus produced, together with the residents' pensions, annuities
and Social Security benefits, is only about one-half of the annual operating costs
of the Homes, we must look to Memorial Gifts, other special gifts during lifetime
and to the generosity of the Brethren and their wives upon their death in order to
sustain our Homes.
The per capita assessment of $1.00 from the dues paid by the Craft is kept at
that nominal figure deliberately for the reason that some Brethren truly cannot
afford any greater amount. Also, it is the philosophy of the Craft that in taking
care of their own, Masons do so voluntarily and in the exercise of Brotherly
·
Love.
The Masonic Homes of California Pooled Income Fund is an outstanding
vehicle by which a Brother may provide for himself or others during his (or
another's) lifetime and, in addition, receive immediate tax advantages as well as
tax advantages upon the death of the lifetime beneficiaries.
Information regarding the Pooled Income Fund, Memorial Gifts and other
gifts and bequests is always available through the Secretary's office. The
continued operation of the Homes depends upon your concern for your Brethren
and it is urged that you ask us if you or your attorney need any assistance in your
financial planning.

Our praise also is for Brothers J. Burton Brown and Gail David and for the
loyal staff at Decoto whose untiring efforts and devotion bridged the gap
resulting from the change in administration at that Home.

102

SUMMARY
The members of the Board of Trustees are grateful to Grand Master Meyer,
not only for his previous service as a trustee, but also for his wisdom and
leadership and in assisting, supporting and guiding the Board in some most
difficult situations.
To Grand Secretary Edward H. Siems, we give our special thanks. His
knowledge of the history of our Homes is unsurpassed and of immeasurable
assistance in steering the desired course for our policy-making duties. His spirit
of cooperation and sincere compassion for our residents and understanding of
Masonry in general is an inspiration to all of us.
Grand Treasurer Chester R. MacPhee provides us with ongoing information
to insure the fiscal responsibility of our operations. He keeps us ever mindful of
our Masonic obligation to provide care and comfort for the residents of the
Homes and of our obligation to do so within prudent financial limitations. His
willingness to devote his time and talent in the handling of our Northern
California real estate transactions in addition to his many other activities on
behalf of Masons and others is sincerely appreciated.

Our objective is to keep our residents functioning at their optimum capacity.
Fortunately, we have the facilities and staff to provide three major levels of care.
As of June 30, 1975, we had 172 residents in Residential Care, 67 in Personal
Care, and 127 in Skilled Nursing Care.
Skilled Nursing Care. Our licensed capacity is 167 beds. The average daily
census (including temporary patients) was 147.8, compared with 157.4 for the
previous year. There were 54,419 nursing patient days; 4,622 doctors calls;
2,688 resident out-patient visits to our Home Clinic; 1,934 visits to specialists at
the Palo Alto Clinic; 3,287 treated by our Podiatrist; and 72 admitted to Stanford
Hospital. There were 615 admissions to, and 619 discharges from, our Skilled
Nursing Facility.
Our most senior resident, Teresa Locke, celebrated her 109th birthday on
November 30, 1974. Mrs. Locke is alert and happy, and we are all looking
forward to her l lOth. She is a resident in our Skilled Nursing Facility.
The age of romance is not past-three resident couples were united in
marriage at the Home: Mrs. Ada Weinberg and Mr. Howard Hermans, Mrs.

II. REORGANIZATION
Mr. Jack D. Billingsley, our Executive Director, with the approval of the
Board of Trustees, reorganized our operational program to consist of five service
departments-Health, Dietary, Facility, Resident, and General-and a Business
Office, all functioning under the Administrator who is responsible to the
Executive Director and the Board of Trustees. The objective is to decentralize
management, and has resulted in Department Directors participating more
meaningfully and responsibly in the planning and in the operations of the Home.
We have added to our Skilled Nursing Staff an Activities Coordinator who
has her degree and is trained as an occupational therapist. She has organized Arts
and Crafts, activities, and programs for our residents both on an individual and
group basis, and has coordinated well with the individual health care plan for
each resident.
III POLICIES AND PROCEDURES

We are well along toward completion of our new Policy and Procedures
Manual for our Skilled Nursing Facility, and we have a good start on our Manual
for Residential Care. A well-defined manual is required by State and Federal
Regulations and Codes.

IV. BUILDINGS
A great deal of time has been spent planning and arranging for work to be
done to make our facilities more attractive, safe, and comfortable for our
residents.
Necessary work to bring our facilities up to required Fire and Life Safety
Standards has been completed.
The contract for carpeting corridors and public areas of Main Building and
Adams Hall, floors 2, 3, and 4, has been let. And, we are going ahead with plans
to paint these areas and also the Skilled Nursing Facility.
New refrigerated drinking fountains have been installed on each floor of the
Main Building .
The old Nurse's Quarters have been converted for use by our Maintenance
Department as a workshop and storage area.
V. DIETARY
In October 1973, the need to move from our old dining room and kitchen, and
the subsequent move to the safe, but less adequate, location in the Main Building
complicated considerably the management of our Food Service Department.

106

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

During this past year, the rehabilitation and fire and life safety work at the Home
placed additional demands on Management. As a consequence, by the decision
of the Board of Trustees, in October 1974, we contracted with a food service
management company to operate our Food Service Program.
VI. PROGRAMS AND ACTIVITIES
Many programs have been put on at the Home for the entertainment of our
Residents; the Cadillac-La Salle Club and their vintage cars is now an annual
event; the San Leandro Musicians' Union performs five times yearly for our
dances and special days. Travelogues and sing-a-longs are provided by various
individuals, including residents. Special trips enjoyed by everyone were to the
Ice Follies, A's ball games, Grand National Horse Show at the Cow Palace,
Alameda County Fair, and to the Sunset House. Of course, our Arts and Crafts
program continues to be of major interest to our Residents. We enjoyed visitors
from 21 different States and from 6 foreign countries: Sweden, Fiji Islands,
Japan, Canada, England and the Philippines.
VII. APPRECIATION
The generous contributions of time, money, donated items, talents and
concern of many Lodges, Eastern Star Chapters, DeMolay Chapters, Rainbow
Girls, Job's Daughters, other affiliated Masonic Bodies, and individual Brothers
and friends make the work of our Home possible. The East Bay Past Matrons'
Association added the 62nd consecutive annual milestone to their history of
putting on "Jam and Jelly Day" at the Home. Their plans are complete to be
with us again this year. To all of these, we are most grateful for brightening the
lives of our Residents.
I am especially appreciative of the inspired leadership and guidance given by
our Grand Master, the Board of Trustees, our Grand Secretary, and our
Executive Direc~or; my sincere thanks to them for their many hours of dedicated
labor given to the Home.
We welcome the opportunity to be of service to our Masonic Brethren and
families in any way possible; and extend to them a cordial invitation to visit
Decoto whenever they can.
Respectfully submitted
JOSEPH M. OLAFSON, Administrator

Mark Paul Baltimore to Phoenix, Ariwna, to live with father and family.
Our children, except for a few colds, scratches, and poison oak have been
healthy and happy. However, we lost one boy, Richard Hudgin, age 17, James
H. Kew Lodge #766 in an accident. This accident resulted in Richard's death,
November 19, 1974. This was a very sobering event to us all, but drew the
children closer together by facing and accepting this sad reality in their young
lives.
Christmas is always a big event at the Masonic Home for Children, and last
Christmas was no exception. Santa Claus, Brother Herb Cooper, who serves
every year as Santa at the gift giving, presided as usual. Every child waits until
each has received his or her gifts-then watch the gay wrappings fly in all
directions! What happy faces!
April brought our Alumni out in force with a huge family picnic on our
grounds. A great time was had reminiscing! Lunch, refreshments, and yamswapping, from noon till seven p.m. kept everyone happy.
It was about this time of year that we received notice that we were to receive
two small buses from the Job's Daughters of California, in an all out fund raising
on behalf of the children here at the Masonic Home. What a great gift! Our vans
get constant use-we really needed new ones. Our children are very proud to be
riding in their bright blue and white 8 and 15 passenger Dodge buses. Thanks to
Job's Daughters and especially Dorothy Boswell, Grand Guardian, and Brother
Robert Sherwood, Associate Grand Guardian.

and other assorted groups including Past Matrons-Patrons Groups, Silver Slippers, Noblettes, etc. etc. We have really enjoyed them, and many have plans for
return engagements.

109

We are happy to announce that Brother Burt Brown has been selected as
Assistant Administrator at DeCoto, although we miss him. We are currently
seeking a replacement.
Staff turnover has been minimal this past year, although several persons have
moved on to better paying jobs.
It is gratifying and heartwarming to observe the continuous benefits presented
to our children through the dedicated efforts of the Masonic affiliated groups. As
a result of these donations, our boys and girls have received special sports
equipment, interesting and valuable stamps for their collections, tickets to
outstanding events (i.e., plays, movies, sports events, circuses), ponies and
riding equipment, picnics with clowns, puppet shows, and other specialized
entertainment. All of these contributions have helped provide special and
memorable events in the lives of our youngsters.
We extend to our many brethren and friends an invitation to visit Covina
when time permits. We are grateful to the Board of Trustees and the Masons of
California and Hawaii for their continued interest and support.

Respectfully submitted,
JAMES C. BLAINE, Administrator

RECOGNITION TO LODGE SECRETARIES

Through the efforts of the Secretaries, our literature is mailed to the members.
We extend our sincere thanks to them, as they play a vital roll in the success of
our program.
RECOGNITION FOR SPECIAL GIFTS

Each year we have Brethren who have given the Endowment Fund substantial
gifts to support the Homes, and give them our sincere thanks. We would like to
encourage our members to consider this method of expressing their devotion to
the support of our Homes.
PRINTED MATERIALS FOR DISTRIBUTION

We encourage each Lodge to avail themselves of the attractive and informative literature on display in the exhibit area. We feel the proper distribution to our
members is the means of informing them of the activities and work of our
Homes, and encourages their support.
SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS

There is still great need for sizeable sums to be used in the rehabilitation
program at Decoto, and we urge our Brethren to give this their earnest
consideration.
SERVICE ROLL CERTIFICATES

The tabs for those Lodges who made the 1975 Service Roll will be sent to the
Lodges for placement on the Certificates. Those Lodges who made the list for the
first time, will receive a Certificate. The average contribution of $3.00 is
required.

We thank our Grand Master, the Most Worshipful Burton Meyer, Jr., for his
leadership and tremendous support in bringing the message to our members
throughout the Jurisdiction.
We express our thanks to the Grand Lodge officers, past Grand Masters and
Grand Lodge Committeemen for their support. To the Grand Lecturer, Assistant
Grand Lecturers, Masters, Wardens and Endowment Committee, for their part in
helping to encourage our Brothers to participate in this worthy program.
We especially thank the Grand Lodge office for their assistance, our Grand
Secretary Edward H. Siems, and Assistant Grand Secretary Verne W. Hendrix.
The efficient staff has been invaluable to the success of our program.
We are also most grateful to the 103,371 Brethren who contributed
$1,040,800.41 to the Permanent Endowment Fund.
It is a rewarding experience to be a part of this endeavor to bring happiness
and security to those in our Homes. Each member of the Board is to be
commended for his dedication to the Endowment program. "It's a Good
Feeling!''
Respectfully Submitted

was established and all agreed that these meetings have proven valuable to both
the officers of the Bureau and to the members of the Board. Other meetings were
held during Grand Lodge Week; on May 17, 1975, to review the budgets of all
the Bureaus; and the other meeting was held on June 25, 1975, with the members
of the Richmond Masonic Service Bureau.
During the group meetings held in Northern and Southern California emphasis was made on the methods that the Service Bureaus could use to assist and
to promote the three Masonic Youth Groups.
POLICY

Upon advice of the Taxation Committee, it was recommended the Bureau
records and files not be housed in the same location with other business records
of the Executive Secretary of the Bureau.
The rule which limits the term of office of a Representative to a Bureau from
the member Lodge was re-studied and not changed from the present six years of
continuous service.
TAXES

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipfal Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

Your Board of Control has enjoyed a most pleasant relationship with the
Officers of the nineteen Masonic Service Bureaus in this great jurisdiction during
the past year. This is our opportunity to pay tribute to those dedicated Freemasons
who give of their time working with the Bureaus. These men continue year after
year to do so much in relieving the distresses of Sojourners, their widows and
orphans who are visiting or residing in the area served by the Bureau.
A summary of all correspondence from the Board of Control to and from
Service Bureaus and Lodges was sent to the Junior Grand Warden and members
of the Board of Control. Copies of the minutes of the meetings were sent to these
people as well as the Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Grand Wardens and
the Grand Secretary.
All official actions of the Board of Control were submitted to the Grand
Master for his approval prior to placing them in effect.
The Right Worshipful Donald B. McCaw, Junior Grand Warden, was
appointed as Liason Officer to the Board of Control by the Grand Master, and
was of most valuable assistance. His counsel assisted the Board in its deliberations on several important matters.
MEETINGS

The Board held five meetings during the year. Two of the meetings were a
group type, one held in Northern California and the other in Southern California.
The officers of all Bureaus were invited to attend. A two-way communication

All Bureaus have filed information returns to the IRS on Form 990 and to the
Franchise Tax Board on either Form 199 or l 99B. Those Bureaus requiring other
tax reports have prepared and filed the reports.
The office of the Grand Secretary made available its facilities to process
quarterly and annual tax returns for the payrolls of all Service Bureaus.
The Board of Control expresses appreciation to W. Stanley Davis, Chairman
of the Taxation Committee for his continued advice and assistance on tax matters
as they apply to•the Service Bureaus.
AUDITS

Audits of the financial and administrative activities of the following Bureaus
were made:
San Jose
Richmond
Santa Monica Bay
Stockton
Santa Barbara
San Diego

UNIFORM COMPACTS

As the result of the relocation of the meeting place, Hermann.Lodge No. 127
withdrew from the San Francisco Bureau, and Saint Elmo Lodge No. 697
withdrew from the East Bay Bureau.
Charity Lodge No. 362 joined the San Jose Bureau. Brotherhood Lodge No.
375 signed a new compact which was required as the result of the consolidation
of Richmond and Military Service Lodges. New compacts were executed to
replace missing compacts from the Bakersfield Bureau by Caledonia Lodge No.
486 and Bakersfield Lodge No. 225.

146

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
ANNUAL REPORTS

All Bureaus have supplied the annual reports, Election, Budget, Statistical
and Financial returns (see appendices).
NEW SECRETARIES

Edward D. Courtney, Secretary of the San Gabriel Bureau passed away in
January 1975 and was replaced by Charles W. Barker. Paul MacQuiddy,
Secretary of the Santa Barbara Bureau retired and was replaced by C. A. Leslie .
Stephen R. Millar retired as Secretary of the Glendale Bureau and was replaced
by A. A. Muske. John A. Crosby retired as Secretary of the Los Angeles Bureau
after serving 23 years and was replaced by Lee 0. Schrock.
GENERAL LETTER

The Chairman of the Board of Control addressed a letter dated April 28 , 1975
to the Masters of all California Lodges and the Secretaries of all Service Bureaus.
This letter outlined the responsibility of Masters and Secretaries to the C.M.C.
with reference to conducting funeral services, and investigations for Sojourners.
Also, their attention was called to the Rules and Regulations under which the
Service Bureaus operate.
INSURANCE

Each Bureau was requested to prepare a complete inventory of all equipment
owned by the Bureau and forward it to Thompkins and Company, for insurance
purposes.
PENSIONS

Employees of all Bureaus not now covered by a pension were advised of the
new Pension Reform Action of 1974, wherein it is now possible to establish their
own retirement plan.
BUSH MASONIC RELIEF

The Board of Control again expresses deep appreciation to Ralph H. Head,
President of the Bush Masonic Relief, and the Directors who serve with him.
This Corporation provides funds for the operation of the six Masonic Service
Bureaus . in the Greater Los Angeles Area.
APPRECIATION

The Board expresses appreciation to all the Executive Secretaries , the
President and the Officers and Committeemen of all the Bureaus for their
dedicated work during the past year. Special appreciation is extended to the
Grand Master, the Grand Secretary and his staff and to all of the Grand Lodge
Officers.

147

The Board expresses appreciation for the time and talent given by Ray L.
Peterson, Sr., who retired in October 1974 from the Board. We welcome Frank
D. Rosen, a new member of the Board and appreciate the contribution he has
made.
The Board of Control functioned within its budget this past year and
herewith requests the sum of $1,300.00 to cover expenses during the ensuing
year.
Respectfully submitted ,
WARREN W. WILDMAN, Chairman
JOSEPH L. OUSLEY
FRANK D. ROSEN

ARTHUR R . KIRK , Secretary

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
After reviewing the Grand Master's Annual Message, the Reports of the
Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary, Grand Lecturer, Masonic Homes Trustees
and the Masonic Homes Endowment Board, the Committee on Distribution
submits the following report:
GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

The Grand Master's Message contains five recommendations and three
decisions. We recommend that the subject matter involved in the Grand Master's
Message be referred to Committees as follows:
Recommendation number one that the Masters of the Lodge or Lodges
consolidating who do not become Master of the consolidated Lodge become Past
Masters of the consolidated Lodge, be referred to The Committees on Policy and
General Purposes and Jurisprudence.
Recommendation number two with regard to the suspension of the Master of
Canoga Lodge No. 611 be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
Recommendation number three with regard to the Master of San Dimas
Lodge No. 428 be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence .
Recommendation number four' regarding illegal coaching and raising of a
Mason of Mizpah Lodge No. 378 be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence .
Recommendation number five concerning use of Lodge funds for Bicentennial community programs be referred to the Committees on Finance and
Jurisprudence. •
Decision number one of the Grand Master regarding the physical qualifications of a prospective Candidate for the Degrees be referred to the Committee on
Ritual.
Decision number two of the Grand Master that it is permissible for members
of the Order of DeMolay, Rainbow for Girls and Job's Daughters to engage in
the sale of tickets to any Shrine-sponsored Football Game, be referred to the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
Decision number three of the Grand Master that it is a proper expenditure of
Lodge Refreshment Funds for the defraying of expenses in connection with a
no-host function provided that the Lodge had approved a motion of this
expenditure from the Refreshment Fund at a Stated Meeting in the month
preceding the month in which the event is to be held and with the amount of
expenditure per member specified in the motion and that the cost be reasonable
and charge for alcoholic beverages not included, be referred to the Committee on
Jurisprudence .
GRAND TREASURER'S REPORT

We recommend that this report be referred in its entirety to the Committee on
Finance.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

GRAND SECRETARY'S REPORT

Masonic Foundation, and the functions of the Committee on Public Schools and
the Committee on Constitution Observance. While there may not have been
state-wide interest, every Lodge event of importance reported to the magazine
during the past year has been published. In addition, emphasis has been placed
on original articles, written by California Masons, pertaining to the history of
California and the part Freemasonry has played in the growth and progress of the
state.
But no magazine can be better than its readers adjudge it to be. It is hoped that
during the coming year the Officers and members of the Constituent Lodges will
let the Publication Board know how the California Freemason can better serve
the more than 215,000 members of California Lodges.
During the past year the per capita for the magazine has been 40 cents, or IO
cents per issue per member. We would recommend that the per capita remain the
same for the succeeding year.

We recommend that the portions of this report be referred to the Committees
as follows:
1. That portion relating to changes of meeting places to the Committees on
Charters and on By-laws.
2. That portion relating to consolidation of Lodges to the Committee on
Charters.
GRAND LECTURER'S REPORT

We recommend that the portions of this report be referred to the Committees
as follows:
1. That portion of the report relating to new programs to encourage membership participation be referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
2. That portion relating to the budget be referred to the Committee on
Finance.

REPORT OF CALIFORNIA FREEMASON
PUBLICATION BOARD
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The publication and distribution of the California Freemason is administered
by a Board comprised of the Grand Master, the Grand Secretary, such advisors as
may be desirable, and an Editor-in-Chief, appointed by the Grand Master.
The magazine has now completed its 22nd year of publication. In the twelve

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Correspondence Committee submits this report for 1975.
We must first note, with great regret, the unfortunate death of Worshipful
Brother George Burch, long the Chairman of this Committee.
In 1974 the then Grand Master wrote Brother George: "Your dedication and
willingness to work for the cause of Freemasonry is most appreciated. The
members of the Grand Lodge Committees are leaders in their respective communities. They are the willing volunteers and you are truly a leader of leaders."
The Grand Master was most happy to reappoint Brother Burch as Chairman of
the Correspondence Committee, as was our present Grand Master. Early this
year Brother Burch passed away. He was a devoted, sincere, effective Chairman,
active in Masonry in the Los Angeles area, including the Scottish Rite bodies
there. We all miss him greatly and are very sorry indeed that he is with us no
more.
Most of you know that the duty of this committee is to review the proceedings
of the other Grand Lodges in our country, extract from them items that we think
may be of special interest to California Masons and submit our reviews to the
editor of the California Freemason for possible publication. This year a few

157

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

reports of Grand Lodges outside the United States have been sent to us; we have
reviewed a very few of these.
This is a pleasant and rewarding activity, tho' sometimes a tedious one. We
are strongly impressed by the scope, variety and worthiness of the activities of
other jurisdictions. We see in them strong evidence of the wide scope, viability
and universality of Freemasonry. Truly, in every country and every clime are
Masons to be found, all of them involved in doing good things for their
communities and for the world, and all devoted to the same high principles of
brotherly love, relief and truth; and committed to temperance, fortitude, prudence and justice.
Much of each and all of the reports is occupied with activities much like our
own. Nearly all have Masonic Homes; many supply scholarships to students,
often managed by endowment funds; they support public schools in many ways;
they support the constitution of the United States, or of the established governments of their own country; this year nearly all of them, or all in this country,
plan to celebrate the Bicentennial of the United States, some of them quite
elaborately; many have membership and Lodge attendance problems, as we do,
and there is some evidence of a slowing down of membership losses; they
support youth groups and associated bodies of many kinds.
Taken together they show how closely Masonic activities are related, how the
basic principles are the same the world over. These kinds of activities we do not
report, rather we take them for granted. They add up to the kind of a Fraternity
with which all of us are proud to be associated.
We do report a very few things that we think are noteworthy. These and
similar things are published in the quarterly issues of the California Freemason.

original 13 states.

occupy them during the builder's lifetime. On his death they become the property

This year our Masonic Temple celebrated its seventeenth birthday. At each
Annual Communication many members of the Fraternity attend Grand Lodge for
the first time. We believe that it is appropriate to remind them that this
magnificent building is our first Grand Lodge Temple, conceived and built by
California Masons as their permanent headquarters. Its conception and momentous birth required eleven years filled with great vision, frustration and finally
satisfactory achievement. It can be truly said that when our Brethren determined
to build a building of their own, they let no obstacles interfere with their
magnificent dream. Masons have from time immemorial been called builders of
beautiful edifices. We truly practice what we teach.
Our California Masonic Memorial Temple, located at the top of prestigious
Nob Hill, has each year added to its glowing reputation as an outstanding
complex for the cultural, civic and educational activities of this great metropolitan city. The building represents our very substantial contribution to the beautification of San Francisco and the promotion of the fine arts and sciences. May the
Great Architect of the Universe grant that this structure will always shine as a
beacon light of our Fraternity's determination to support and advance a free
public school system for the education of the generations of Americans yet to be
and of our determination to make the world a better place for all people in which
to live.
Acoustically, our auditorium has no equal for concerts, lectures and the
performance of musical and dramatic presentations. Business organizations,
fraternal societies, state governmental departments and professional associations
are continually increasing their use of our facilities for their meetings and trade
shows. It is an excellent showcase for all their diverse and numerous activities.

TOURS AND VISITATIONS

The Temple is open daily, except Saturday and Sunday, for visitors from 8:45
A.M. to 4:45 P.M. If there are other activities in the Temple on Saturday or
Sunday, then additional tours are arranged if necessary. We have had guests from
every one of the 50 states and from many of the countries of the world visiting
our Temple. This year we were hosts to visitors from the following foreign
countries:

Our staff has been requested to make every effort to give that extra excellence
in service and attention to our tenants which results in their repeated use of our
facilities. This continuous fine cooperation not only builds a better image of our
Fraternity but also makes the use of our fine facilities more enjoyable for our
tenants. Many of these tenants have commented most favorably in unsolicited
letters of this unusual anticipated attention to their diverse and unique needs.
TEMPLE STAFF

Members of the craft from all the 50 States and from many foreign countries
request information to take home to their respective Blue Lodges. They are
amazed at the pristine beauty of our Temple . We learn continually that we are a
unique grand jurisdiction and a leader in the activities of Freemasonry.
Many representatives of Senior Citizens groups, Rainbow for Girls, Job's
Daughters, DeMolay Chapters and other concordant bodies have arranged for
tours of our beautiful building. Hundreds of public school children visit our
Temple. These young people gain a lasting impression of our determination to
help them achieve their potential of a better life through free public school
education. Likewise, the many graduation exercises held this year in our Temple
are proof of the public's appreciation of our beautiful building and its contribution to the most auspicious occasion of graduation.
MAINTENANCE AND IMPROVEMENTS

Nothing less than the highest standards of maintenance will continue to
preserve the classic beauty of our Temple. After 17 years of use and occupancy,
some of the mechanical equipment will, of necessity, require replacement or
modernization. The elevators needed further locks and newer directional controls, the hot water boiler tubes required repairs and replacement, the Pine Street
ramp required renovation to protect the metal panel. All of these needed repairs
were undertaken and completed. All portions of the building not faced with
marble must be painted. The exterior marble facing must be cleaned after so
many years of use to remove the embedded grime to prevent deterioration of the
surface. This work could not be done until after the apartment building being
built next door was ready for its tenants' occupancy. That building is now
completed. Interior painting, stripping and waxing is a continual necessity to not
only preserve the charm and usefulness of our building, but also to protect the
surface from erosion through constant wear and tear. All of this interior
maintenance was undertaken and done during the past year by our own staff to
reduce the cost of operations.
PuBLIC RELATIONS AND avic AFFAIRS

Membership in the Nob Hill Association, the San Francisco Convention and
Visitors Bureau, the Press Club of San Francisco and the Greater San Francisco
Chamber of Commerce serves us as a much needed contact with prominent civic
and business leaders from whom many rental prospects and much useful
information of value can be obtained.

Our manner of operation requires only a small, loyal, creative and capable
staff. Without their dedication, it would be impossible to meet the many
challenges and trying problems that continually arise in the management of an
edifice such as ours under present competitive conditions. We sincerely appreciate their past services and helpful assistance. They have made creative
service more than just an expression.
George Gavin became our General Manager in 1963. During the past 12
years, thanks to his unselfish devotion to the duties of his position, the income of
the Temple has shown a continuous growth. We extend our grateful thanks to
him as our Executive Vice-President and General Manager, for his contribution
to the successful operation of the Temple.
Every successful organization must have management in depth to assure a
continuous smooth operation of the transfer of responsibility in the event of
retirement or illness of personnel. We have accordingly recently authorized the
employment of an Assistant Manager. In addition to providing management in
depth, this will strengthen our rental department and increase our revenue by
soliciting usage of our facilities from new potential users.
During the past year the rental income from the building and garage increased
despite adverse economic conditions. The garage income will always continue to
fluctuate because it is largely based on the occupancy created from the use of the
auditorium and exhibition space. This increased use of our facilities means more
income from this important source.
Through judicious management the operating expenses, salaries, supplies,
repairs, maintenance, including real and personal taxes, increased only
moderately.
OCCUPANCY

During the past year our Auditorium, because of its excellent facilities,
location and acoustical properties, has been used for some of the finest concert
and theatrical-type of performances. This has enhanced the fine reputation of the
Te~ple .as a place of culture and refinement befitting the admirable image of
Cal1fom1a Freemasonry. Your Trustees believe this type of use of our premises
should be continually encouraged.
A number of new hotels and additions with the most modem of convention
facilities have been completed in the past year. We have to be cognizant that each
new facility is and will be competitive for our rental clientele insofar as
Exhibition Hall and Auditorium use are concerned.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

With this in mind, your Trustees believe it is most desirable that the present
policy of diversified rental of the Auditorium and Exhibit Hall be followed. This
is a protection against the reduced use of either one by the booking of only one
form of tenancy. Each new hotel will encourage and bring some additional
convention business to San Francisco, thus increasing the City' s reputation as an
ideal place to hold meetings.
Our Auditorium is well adapted to all kinds of stockholder, professional and

and organizations that have used the Auditorium and Exhibit Hall for important
meetings.
It is most gratifying that well known educational institutions of higher
learning have held their graduation exercises in our building because of its beauty
and impressive dignity. The setting contributes to the historic occasion.
The State of California uses our Exhibit Hall for the examinations conducted
for Certified Public Accountants . The State Bar of California also holds its bar
examinations in our premises.

INSURANCE
The Grand Lodge Insurance Committee has reviewed all insurance coverage of
the Temple and the Pine Street properties and has approved them as proper and
appropriate for the purposes intended.
PINE STREET PROPERTIES
During the past year these properties were again inspected by the code
enforcement authorities of the City and County of San Francisco and we have
complied with all their recommendations. The present cash flow still justifies .the
maintenance of the old buildings as a source of revenue, until a more appropnate
use of the land can be determined.
This year it was necessary that the exterior of all the Pine Street properties be
painted. During the early part of this year construction continued on the luxury
17 story apartment house immediately West of the Temple. It has now been
completed and has 270 apartments in an L-shaped design surrounding a courtyard. Through the efforts of counsel of the Board of Trustees, an agreement was
negotiated prior to its construction that protects our Temple for any future needed
expansion in height.
Your Trustees have always been committed to a policy of fiscal responsibility. We are pleased to report that we have no indebtedness except ordinary
operational expenses which are currently paid as incurred.
We will continue to study the best economic and feasible use of the Pine
Street properties. Your Trustees will be guided in their deliberations by the
possible demands and needs for further expansion of our present facilities and the
good of the Fraternity. We will keep the general membership advised of our
progress in this regard.

REPORT OF RETIREMENT PENSION
PLAN COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F . & A. M. of California:
In addition to the usual duties required of the Retirement Pension Plan
Committee, in i;onnection with the administration of the California Masonic
~etirement Plan, we ha~e been concerned this past year with changes to be made
m the Plan-cha nges imposed by reason of the new Employee Retirement
Income Security Act of 1974.
We are advised that amendments necessary to conform our Plan to require~en~s imposed by the new law must be completed by January 1, 1976. This
impl~es approval by regul~tory agencies regularly charged with supervision of
pension plans, together with the U. S. Department of Labor to which has been
assigned jurisdiction over regulations in the new Pension Reform Law.
Oll!" firm of actuaries, Coates and Crawford, which prepares our annual
actuanal reports , has been represented at all meetings of the committee by Barrett
N . Coates, Jr. and he is now engaged in the final preparation of amendments
necessary to bring our Plan into compliance with the Pension Reform Law of
1974.
Our Retirement Pension Plan operates on a calendar year basis and reports for
the year ended December 31 , 1974 furnished by the Grand Lodge Accounting
Department, the Certified Public Accountants, the Trustee for the Plan, Wells
Fargo Bank and the Actuaries, Coates and Crawford, have been reviewed. Also
available to the Committee were monthly statements prepared by Alliance

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Capital Management Corporation, investment counsellors to the Grand Lodge
Committee on Investments which supervises investments for the Pension Plan .
As of December 31, 1974, trust assets, allowing for certain year-end accruals,
amounted to $1,626,306 on a cost basis as compared to $1,530,411 on December
31, 1973-an increase of $95,895 for the calendar year 1974. This increase
occured by way of employer and employee contributions and from net investment income, less trust expenses, pension payments, refunds to resigning
members and a realized loss on a sale of securities. Of the total Fund Balances of
$1,626,306 , $1,233,041 is assignable to the Masonic Homes of California and
$393,262 is assignable to the Grand Lodge of California and its component
organizations.
The market value of trust securities on December 31, 1974 was $983,730, a
decline of $631,451 from cost. This compares with a decline of $324,539 in
market value as reported for December 31, 1973. As of June 30, 1975,
improvement in the security market had reduced the decline to approximately
$490,000.
As noted in previous reports of this Committee, income from investments,
together with employer and employee contributions, has been more than necessary to discharge pension obligations, pay operating expenses of the Plan and to
maintain necessary reserves. Changes currently being made in the portfolio of
securities are designed to afford safety of capital and to increase yield.
For the calendar year 1974, investment income totaled $83,537 and expenses
charged to the Plan for trustees' fees, actuarial services, audit fees and interest on
refunds of employee contributions totaled $11 ,580. There was, in addition, a loss
of $16, 119 on sale of securities leaving a net investment income for the year of
$55,838 which is equivalent to a yield of 3.57% on the cost value of invested
funds . If the yield were computed on the basis of excluding expenses charged to
the Plan, the yield on a cost basis would be 4.33%.
Comparative yields for the preceeding year (1973) were 4.57% and 5.17%,
respectively. Using figures determined by Wells Fargo Bank, Trustee for the
Plan, the expected average investment yield for 1975 on the portfolio of
securities on the December 31 , 1974 cost basis should be 5.6% and the yield on a
market basis should approximate 7. 2% .
The valuations established by the actuaries for the purpose of determining the
employer contribution rate have been made on the assumption that the Trust will
continue to earn 4% per annum.
A review of schedules contained in the actuaries' report shows that for the
Masonic Homes of California the number of active members enrolled in the Plan
decreased from 113 to 110. The annual covered payroll decreased by
$20,034-f rom $799,860 to $779,826. The annual average salary of employees
participating in the Plan increased from $7,078 to $7,089 as of January 1, 1975.
The number of retired members decreased by I-from 37 to 36 and the annual
.
pensions being paid decreased from $29,069 to $28,472.
For the Grand Lodge of California and its components, the number of active
members in the Plan decreased by three-from 18 to 15. The annual covered
payroll decreased by $10,870-f rom $149,201 to $138,331. The average annual

salary increased from $8,289 to $9,222. The number of retired members
increased from 15 to 20 and the annual pensions being paid increased from
$19,656 to $23,751-a s of January 1, 1975.
To maintain the Plan in sound financial condition, continuing the employee
contribution rate of 3%, assuming a 4% return on investments and considering
the portfolio of investments at cost value as of December 31, 1974, our actuaries
have calculated the employer contribution rate necessary to maintain current
service benefits accruing under the Plan.
For the Masonic Homes of California, the contribution rate is expressed as
8.17% of payroll. For the Grand Lodge of California, the contribution rate is
expressed as 10.58% of payroll. For the preceeding year, the corresponding rates
were 8.88% and 10.83%, respectively.
We recommend approval of the employer contribution rates as determined by
the actuaries.

REPORT OF CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
Because we still find a lack of knowledge among the Brethren as to the
nature, objects, purposes and activities of the California Masonic Foundation, it
seems appropriate, at this time, to endeavor to clarify once and for all some of the
misunderstanding which have previously existed.
First of all, it is an independent non-profit corporation, which was organized
under the laws of California in 1969. It has been granted a private foundation tax
exemption by the Internal Revenue Service. The governing body consists of
fifteen directors, who are called Trustees. Each member of this Board of Trustees
is nominated by the Grand Master for a three year term, except the Deputy Grand
Master, who is elected for the year he serves in that office. To maintain
continuity the terms are staggered.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The officers consist of a President, Vice President, a Treasurer and an
Assistant Treasurer, and a Secretary and an Assistant Secretary. The Grand
Treasurer also serves as our Treasurer, and the Grand Secretary serves as our
Secretary. Neither is a member of our Board. Accounting functions are handled
through the Grand Secretary's office and investments are handled by the
Investment Committee of Grand Lodge.
So much for what we are. Now, what we are not.
We are not a Scholarship Committee; we are not even a Committee. It is true
that so far the majority of our funds have been used, each year, for the
scholarship grants to worthy students, who are in financial need . We have a
Scholarship Committee, composed of five members of the Board of Trustees,
and they review all applications for scholarship very carefully.
All charitable grants, both scholarship and others, are made on a statewide
basis insofar as possible. In most cases, if a Lodge has recommended a
successful applicant, a presentation ceremony is scheduled at the Lodge, to
which event the relatives and friends are invited. This has resulted in much
favorable comment, both by word-of-mouth and in newspapers.
However, in addition to scholarship awards, our income, which averages
some $65,000 to $70,000 per year, and which is derived from assets valued at
over $1,000,000, is used for several other types of charitable projects. Our aim is
to benefit all mankind, as is provided by our By-Laws, and this we endeavor to
do, not only by assisting worthy students to obtain an education, but also by
furnishing assistance where the need is great and the cause is worthy.
During the past year, charitable grants for all purposes totalled in excess of
$70,000. This was divided as follows:

of Los Angeles, Calif. . ............ . ............ 2,125

The average scholarship grant is $500.00, which is designed to supplement
the student's other sources of funds . In many cases we have received letters from
the students, to whom these awards have been made, stating that they were most
grateful and could not have continued their educations otherwise. Since 1969,
total scholarship awards have been granted to approximately 350 students,
representing some $170,000, which has been awarded to students who are
seeking an education.
Qualifications for students seeking assistance are generally that they be
attending, or ready to attend, a recognized educational institution; that they have
reasonably good grades; and, above all, that they be in real financial need. A
regular application form, which will be furnished on request, must be prepared
and signed by the applicant.
In conclusion, may it be said that while our available income is not unlimited,
our Board is dedicated to making use of it in the best way possible, not only for
the benefit of those individuals and organizations to whom grants are given, but
also for the benefit of Masonry in general. We take pride in being a part of this
organization.
Respectfully submitted,

Fountain Valley in Orange County which has sent out the required 45 day notice
of intention to form a Lodge under the name of Fountain Valley Bicentennial
Lodge. They are hopeful that they can be instituted so that we will have at least
one new Lodge in the coming Bicentennial year. We recommend to the Masons
of Orange County that they assist and encourage this new group.
Population trends in some of our older cities have created problems in
established Lodges that have led to a number of consolidations of Lodges. These
same shifts in population have created new and prosperous communities that
have no Masonic organizations or facilities of any kind. To provide Lodges and
meeting places in these newer areas is one of the major challenges facing our
Fraternity. It would be tragic if the problems of older urban areas should lead to
a negative reaction toward the formation of new Lodges in places where they are
badly needed.
Those of you living in or near communities such as I have described can
perform a great service to Masonry by starting, or assisting, clubs that wish to
form Lodges. Such assistance does not necessarily entail membership in a new
Lodge. Many times help is needed in organizing, in finding a suitable meeting
place, in procuring supplies and equipment, in finances, and in recruiting and
coaching Officers. Needless to say the Committee on Charters also stands ready
to assist in any way possible.
There has been referred to the Committee on Charters, that portion of the
Grand Secretary's Report dealing with various changes of meeting place, and
with the following consolidations of Lodges:
Fairmont Lodge No. 435 and George Washington Lodge No. 525 to be
known as George Washington Lodge No. 435.

George Washington Lodge No. 435 and Hunters Point Naval Lodge No. 706
to be known as George Washington Lodge No. 435.

We find the requirements of the law respecting changes of meeting place and

REPORT OF INVESTMENT COMMITTEE
FOR FISCAL YEAR ENDING JUNE 30, 1975

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
During the past year the stock market staged a rather sharp and broad rally
from its December, 1974 lows and an important part of the previous years
extreme undervaluation was corrected. Also, as long term interest rates declined,
bond prices increased by about 6o/o from a year earlier. These two factors were
important to the investment portfolio under our control, the market value of
which increased to $48,430,885 from $37 ,618,218 at June 30, 1974. The
estimated annual income being earned from the portfolio increased during the
year from $2,455,470 to $2,737,351, a gain of ll1h%.
Activities of the Committee are regulated by the Masonic Code, which sets
forth the three major categories (as groups) of securities allowable for investment. These categories are summarized as follows:
(I) Group I-Consists of cash, savings accounts, obligations of the United
States, obligations of the State of California and it-s political subdivisions, and
such other securities as are legal for savings banks in California and Hawaii. In
general. Group I may be said to consist of the highest grade and most
conservative securities. At least 20% of the funds available for investment must
be maintained in such securities.
(2) Group II-Consists generally of bonds, debentures, and other evidences
of indebtedness which do not meet the qualifications of Group I. It also consists
of preferred stocks which are listed on a National Securities Exchange and the
preferred stocks of corporations whose common stocks are eligible for investment in Group III.
(3) Group III-Consists of common stocks, which must be fully listed and
registered on a national exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange
Commission, bank and insurance company stocks, shares of investment trusts,
and savings accounts with savings and loan associations. Total investments in
Group III securities are generally limited to 60% of the total portfolio.

REPORT OF BOARD OF LIBRARY COMMISSIONERS

Government and high-grade Corporate bonds now represent 35% of the
market value of the portfolio, with the average life of these securities being
somewhat less than 20 years. Quality-wise, the issues held all are rated
investment grade by the various investment rating services.
Convertible debentures and convertible preferred stocks make up 14% of the
portfolio. These issues are currently returning approximately 7% on market
value, and with the improvement in common stock values have increased in price
because of their convertibility into common stocks.
Common stocks continue to represent just over 50% of the fund. Over the past
year, the market value of these securities has increased 11.8%. This was
somewhat greater than the increase during the same period of the Dow Jones
Industrial Average or of the Standard & Poor's 500 Stock Index. At the present
time dividend income of 4.8% is being earned on our common stock portfolio.
