15. Do you promise that you will not apply for or receive any degree or
be initiated in any body, order, or organization the prerequisite of
membership therein is that a person be a Master Mason within Twentyfour months after receiving the degree of Master Mason or until you have
given satisfactory evidence, by strict examination in open Lodge, that you
are entirely proficient and well-qualified in the Candidate's Lecture of the
Degree of Master Mason?
Respectfully submitted,
CHARLES MAXWELL BERG,P.M. No. 797
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and on Policy and General
Purposes.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 13 seeks to amend Question 15 of the Application for
Degrees. The amended question would allow anyone receiving the degree of
Master Mason to petition or receive degrees or be initiated in any body, the
prerequisite being that the person is a Master Mason if:
(a) Twenty-four months have elapsed since he became a Master Mason; or
(b) He had successfully completed the Candidate's Lecture of the Degree of
Master Mason.
As presently worded, Question 15 of the application requires that the Master
Mason must successfully complete the Candidate's Lecture of the Degree of
Master Mason and must wait twelve months after receiving the Degree of Master
Mason before he can petition or receive degrees or be initiated in any body, the
prerequisite being that he is a Master Mason.
At various intervals over the years our Grand Lodge has been asked to amend
Question 15 of the application to remove the requirement of the proficiency in the
Candidate's Lecture of the Degree of Master Mason. Throughout the years each
proponent has argued that the requirements of the proficiency must be relaxed in
order to make Masonry more attractive to those who want to "pass through" the
Masonic Lodge into the Concordant Bodies.
Fortunately, such relaxation of requirements has not occurred. Nor is it the
belief of your Committee on Policy and General Purposes that such relaxation
will really strengthen our Fraternity.
The proponent of this resolution presents a new approach in that he would
have the new Master Mason wait two years before applying for membership in
the Concordant Bodies or pass his Third Degree Proficiency before he applies.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Section 527 of the California Masonic Code sets forth the form of Application
for the Degrees of Masonry and Resolution No. 13 proposes that Question 15 of
this Application be amended to give the candidate a choice between passing a
satisfactory examination in the Candidate's Lecture of the 3rd Degree or waiting
2 years before he can apply for membership in an organization requiring Masonic
membership as a prerequisite.
This differs from our present law in 2 respects.
1. Now the candidate must pass his proficiency in the 3rd Degree Candidate's
Lecture before he can join another Masonic organization and this new
proposal would make this optional if he would prefer to wait 2 years.
2.Now the candidate must wait one year and this new proposal would make
him wait 2 years if he does not pass a satisfactory examination in the
Candidate's Lecture of the 3rd Degree.
To carry out the intent of the proponent your Committee submits the
following:
RESOLVED, that Question No. 15 of Section 527 of California Masonic
Code be amended to read as follows:

"15. Do you promise that you will not apply for or receive any degree or
be initiated in any body, order, or organization the prerequisite of
membership therein is that a person be a Master Mason within twenty-four
months after receiving the degree of Master Mason or until you have given
satisfactory evidence, by strict examination in open Lodge, that you are
entirely proficient and well qualified in the Candidate's Lecture of the
Degree of Master Mason, whichever event shall first occur?"
To place the matter before Grand Lodge we move the adoption of the
Resolution.
Not adopted.

(14)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the encouragement of young men to seek the Degrees of
Masonry is necessary for the continued success of Masonry in California; and
WHEREAS, one of the primary sources of potential members is from the
Order of DeMolay; and
WHEREAS, a sum of money in excess of $100.00 for the application fee in
this Jurisdiction sometimes works a hardship on a deserving applicant at 21 years
of age, thereby proving a negative factor in the motivation of a young man to
seek the Degrees of Masonry.
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that payment of the application fee for the

as is afforded in other Masonic Jurisdictions, and that the California Masonic

HERSCHEL c. DENTON, M., No. 396
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, Finance and on Policy and General
Purposes.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 14 proposes that the payment of the application fee for the
Degrees of Masonry be divided into payment by the Degree. The proponents of
this resolution state that this will encourage young men to seek membership in
Masonry.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that if a man is not
able to pay the entire fee for the Degrees, he is probably financially unable to
afford the other expenses that membership entails. It would be better for both the
Lodge and the man to withhold his application until he could better afford his fee,
his dues and the expense of participating in the other activities of the Lodge.
We do not ascribe to the belief that good members will be attracted by
"bargain events" or "cut-rate incentives." We feel that a better way to attract
new members is by creating favorable impressions of our institution, in the eyes
of the public, by conducting ourselves, in our daily lives, according to the
lessons we have been taught in the Lodge. Also, by our participation in activities
of civic, community and public schools affairs. Let's endeavor to "sell"
Masonry on it's merits, not by financial inducement. Your committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, Finance and on Policy and General
Purposes.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponent of Resolution No. 16 charges that California Masonic L~w
"severely discriminates against our older Masons" and suggests that a hfe
membership actuarial table would correct such inequity as well as reduce losses
in membership caused by suspension for nonpayment of dues for members with
limited incomes which "will not go far enough today."
The present law requires that Lodges who have adopted a system of l~fe
membership establish the fee at a sum of no less than $250.00 for Lodges with
the minimum annual dues of $12.00 and proportionately greater as annual dues
are greater. The fee paid must forever be kept and maintained for a perman~nt
Life Membership Fund, invested according to California Masonic Code Sect10n
574, and only the income therefrom may be used by the Lodge.
The subject of Life Membership Funds and how they should be han?led
appears in many past proceedings of this Grand Lodge. In 1936 the Committee
on Policy and General Purposes reported as follows in response to a proposal at
that time:
"In other words, the proposals are to destroy the requirements now in our
law that life membership funds are perpetual funds and cannot be used for
any purpose except to earn income for the Lodge. The Committee is of the
opinion that those funds are not earned by a Lodge at the time the _life
membership is taken out, nor are they earned by the Lodge at any time
during the member's life. Those funds are to pay a member's dues. They
do not ordinarily realize to the Lodges an income that is as large as the
dues; there is a loss to the Lodge in dues every year. That loss is made up
by the fact that the fund is permanent and no part is paid out at the time of
death of a life member. It is not an earned fund; it is earning money for the
Lodge every year and is a trust fund and should not be dissipated."
Nothing has changed today-dues may rise, inflation takes its toll and ~he
Lodge may use only the income from its Life Membership Fund. If Resolution
No. 16 is approved, the fee required of members for a life membership co~ld be
as small as the stipulated minimum in the resolution-fifty dollars. Obviously
$50.00 cannot earn sufficient interest when invested according to law to pay even
the minimum dues of a member for one year.

234

235

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

A Lodge can exist only if it is fiscally sound. A number of Grand Masters
have opined that it is a privilege for a member to pay dues and help support his
Lodge. It should not be the intent of a life membership fund to enable a member
to escape the duty and privilege of fairly and equitably bearing a share of the
support of his Lodge. A member can be of perpetual assistance to his Lodge if he
subscribes to a Life Membership because the income from the fee he pays forever
belongs to his Lodge. In the opinion of your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes, Resolution No. 16 would not be a fiscally sound policy for Lodges.
You will recall that the proponent of this resolution attributes a share of our
losses in membership in recent years to the fact that some of our older members
have limited incomes which are insufficient for them to pay dues and therefore
these members are suspended for nonpayment of dues.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes would hope that this is not
true.
As it is a duty and privilege for members who are able to pay dues, so is it the
duty of a Lodge to remit the dues of a member who is unable to pay-regardless
of the age or years of service of such a member.
Therefore, the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, recommends a
"No" vote.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCE

Referred to Committees on Policy and General Purposes and on Jurisprudence.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The financial statements prepared by Hurdman and Cranstoun, Certified
Public Accountants, were referred to this Committee, although much too late for
complete review . They have been reproduced in the Grand Treasurer's report,
and this report was reviewed by your Committee on Finance. There is much of
interest in our Grand Treasurer' s report, and the audits incorporated therein,
which are a part of the published proceedings. We extend our appreciation to our
Grand Treasurer and recommend your approval of his report .
The total GQllld Lodge expenditures for the past fiscal year were generally
within the approved budgets. There were, however, some unexpected expenditures for which no provisions had been made, as well as an usual number of items
which exceeded the original estimate, such as Grand Lodge Officers' travel,
veterans' buttons, inventory of Lodge supplies and Workmen's Compensation
insurance. These, together with the publication deficit of the California Freemason Magazine, totalled $54, 175.00, and were duly approved as supplemental
appropriations by the Grand Master. We recommend your approval of his action.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 19 amounts to the final step in what has been a ten-year long
project to revise and update the California Masonic Code. Adoption of this
resolution will give approval to the product of untold hours of devoted labor by
knowledgeable and dedicated members of this Grand Lodge in the revision of our
Masonic Code. We can assure you that any substantive changes which have been
made in the work of Code revision have been minor and have been made for
clarity or to correct ambiguities. Further, there has been a maximum amount of
checking and rechecking of all deletions and modifications. This Grand Lodge
has long wanted and long needed an improved and updated Code. The work has
been completed, and the only practical way to move forward to the use of the
revised Code is by adoption of this resolution.
I therefore move adoption of Resolution No. 19, and your Committee on
Policy and General Purposes strongly recommends a "Yes" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence also urged a "Yes" vote.
Adopted unanimously.

We accordingly offer the following resolution:
RESOLVE D, that for the purpose of paying the expenses of Grand Lodge a
per capita of $3.40 be levied for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1976, divided as
follows:

license fees, and other fixed costs, appears right and proper. However, if a person
uses his automobile only occasionally and incidentally for business purposes, an
amount adequate to cover out-of-pocket costs only, such as gasoline, oil,
replacement of tires and accessories, and normal repairs and maintenance, seems
fair and sufficient.
Your Committee on Finance has concluded that for purposes of reimbursing
Grand Lodge Officers, Staff, Committeemen, Inspectors, etc. for the personal use
of their cars on Grand Lodge business, fixed costs such as depreciation and
insurance, should not be included. Therefore, assuming the operation of a
standard-sized American car, a proper rate of reimbursement for out-of-pocket costs
to persons using their personal automobiles on Grand Lodge business from the close
of this Grand Lodge Communication until the corresponding date in 1976 is set at 11
cents per mile.
The Committee on Finance will hereafter include as part of its regular annual
report the automobile mileage allowance and will also provide guidance on such
other expenditure reimbursements as may appear for the good of the Craft.
We are presently engaged in a study of the pay of members attending Grand
Lodge, but we are not prepared to make recommendation atthis time. Until our study
is completed, the present method of determining representatives' travel allowance
on the basis of 10 cents per mile will be continued.

SUPPLEMENTAL REPORT OF
COMMITTEE ON FINANCE

Recommendation Number 4 of the 1974 Grand Master's Message, concerning
adequate standards of reimbursement for expenditures, was referred to the
Committee on Finance for study and recommendation . We recognize the need for
ongoing study to assure that reimbursement standards be maintained at adequate and
proper levels consistent with ever-changing costs of transportation, meals: and
lodging. Based on our study to date, we are prepared to make a recommendation at
this time as to the mileage reimbursement for the use of personal automobiles on
Grand Lodge busines-s by Grand Lodge Officers, Staff, Committee men, Inspectors,
etc .
Grand Master Ebbage in his Message last year made the statement that "the
allowance of ten cents per mile is hardly more than token repayment and should be
increased.' ' Granted that the present figure may warrant adjustment in the light of
1975 automobile operating costs, we take exception to the comment that it is " hardly
·
more than token repayment ."
In conducting our study, the Committee on Finance availed itself of nationally
recognized and accepted resource materials. Principal reference is the latest study,
published April 1974, by the Highway Statistics Division, Federal Hi~hway
Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation entitled: "Cost of Operatmg an
Automobil e." Supporting data was obtained from the "1975 Business Car
Allowances, Controls and Fleet Management Practices, ' ' by the Dartnell Institute
of Business Research. Also examined was a report in the June 1975 issue of
Changing Times, The Kiplinger Magazine, on " Car Costs in 20 Areas .'' Various
other magazine articles reporting on similar studies were examined and evaluated.
Data was also obtained on the allowances granted by nine major companies when
reimbursing their own employees for business use of their personal automobiles.
Throughout these studies we found strong support for the principle that it is
reasonable and proper to differentiate between the person whose job is dependent
upon owning and using a car on his employer's behalf and the person who may
occasionally and incidentally use his car for business purposes. In the first instance,
reimbursement on the basis of total cost per mile, including depreciation, insurance,

Respectfully submitted,

We have examined the statements of assets, liabilities and
fund balance arising from cash transactions of T_he Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California
(a nonprofit, unincorporated , fra.t ernal organization) as of June 30,
1975 and 1974 and the related statements of revenues and expenses
for the years then ended. Our examinations were made in accordance
with generally accepted auditing standards, and accordingly included
such tests of the accounting records and such other auditing
procedures as we considered necessary in the circumstances.
The market value of common and preferred stock investments
was approximately $292,000 ·or 32~ below their carrying value as of
June 30, 1975· It is not determinable whether this decline is of a
temporary or permanent nature. Any decline in the market value.---0f
bonds is considered temporary since it is generally the policy of the
Grand Lodge to hold bonds until maturity.
In our opinion, subject to the ultimate realization of the
carrying value of common and preferred stocks, the f·inancial
statements identified above present fairly the assets, liabilities and
fund balance arising from cash transactions of The Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California as
of June 30, 1975 and 1974 and revenues and expenses for the years
then ended, on a consistent basis.

1 - Significant Accounting Policies
Basis of Accounting
The financial statements are presented on a modified
cash basis of accounting. Generally, revenues are
recorded at the time of receipt and expenses are
recorded when paid. The liability ie accrued in the
case of certain budgeted expenses which are incurred
before the balance sheet date.
Investments
Investments in securities purchased are carried at
cost and securities received by gift or bequest are
carried at approximate market value on the date
received.
Furniture, Equipment,
and Improvements
Furnittfre and equipment purchased after June 30, 1957
are carried at their historical cost. No depreciation
ie provided on these aseete.
Pension Plan
The Grand Lodge contributes to the California
Masonic Retirement Plan for the benefit of
substantially all full-time employees. Total pension
expense for the years ended June 30, 1975 and 1974
was $8,487 and $7,875, respectively. All prior and
current service costs have been funded. Aseete held
by the Fund at December 31, 1974 were in excess of
vested benefits.
Federal and State Income Taxes
The Grand Lodge ie exempt from Federal and State
income taxes.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

271

MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNIA
NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
June 30, 1975 and 1974

- Significant Accounting Policies
Basis of Accounting
The financial statements are stated on a modified
cash basis of accounting. Generally, revenues are
recorded at the time of receipt and expenses are
recorded when paid, except that payroll and related
costs are recorded when accrued.
Investments
Investments in securities purchased are carried at
cost and securities received by gift or bequest are
carried at approximate market value on the date
received. Unrealized losses due to fluctuations in
the market value of bonds are not recorded because
it is the policy of the trustees generally to hold
bonds to their maturity.
Other Assets
Other assets consist of life insurance policies,
real estate, and mineral rights assigned or
bequeathed to the Masonic Homes. These assets are
recorded at the nominal value of $1 each for
accountability. Payments by the Masonic Homes _of
obligations of the assignors secured by these assets
are added to the nominal value, with the exception
of life insurance premiums which are charged to
expense when paid.
Property
Land, buildings, and equipment are recorded at
original cost and no depreciation is taken.
Additions which represent minor replacements of
property are charged to expense.

MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNIA
NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
June 30, 1975 and 1974
Reserves for Special Purposes
The trustees have established various special
reserves to which are added gifts and bequests
and other amounts which generally are used at
the direction of the trustees for purposes
other than direct operating expenses. The
assets represented by these reserves are
included in the assets of the General Fund.
Federal and State
Taxes on Income
The Masonic Homes is exempt from Federal and
state taxes on income.

2 - Notes Receivable
Notes receivable arise from the sale of real estate assigned
to the Masonic Homes by residents of the Decoto Home and from real
estate received as gifts or bequests.

3 - Restrictions on Trust Funds
John and Lena Luckenbach Fund
The principal of this fund, restricted by the
terms of the Will of the donor, is to be kept
intact and the income used only for the benefit
of the care of orphans or the aged in Masonic
Homes of southern California.
George F and Laura E Brigham Scholarship Fund
The principal of this fund is held as a
Scholarship Fund for the benefit of the Covina
Home residents, of which $25,000 may be loaned
for this purpose. Income of this fund is
restricted and may be used only for providing
scholarships.

272

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNIA
NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
June 30, 1975 and 1974
Walter W Schultz and Maude S Schultz Scholarship Fund
The income from this fund is restricted and may
be used only to provide financial assistance to
needy children for educational purposes.
Mildred R Brown and Leroy G Brown Memorial Fund
Principal and income from this fund are to be
used for making loans for educational purposes
to any children that the Board of Trustees
deems worthy.
Frederick E and Frieda E Sommers Trust
This fund is to be used exclusively for the
education of full orphan children.
George M and Florence G Perine Endowment Fund
The principal of this fund, subject to the
provision included in the Will of the donor
shall be kept intact and only the income
therefrom shall be used . for the benefit of the
Decoto Home.
Harriet C Wadleigh Endowment Annuity Fund
This fund, in the original amount of $30,000
is subject to a contract with the donor
providing for the payment of certain life
annuities out of the principal and income
thereof. Under the terms of the contract,
principal of the fund expended in payment of
the annuities is to be later restored out of
income when the annuities no longer absorb the
entire income. After restoration of the
principal to the original sum of $30,000, the
income from the fund is to be used for the
benefit of the residents of the Covina Home.
Student Aid Fund
This fund is designated by the trustees for use
for student aid.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNIA
NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
June 30, 1975 and 1974
Edmund Clement Atkinson Fund
The principal of this fund, subject to the
provision in the Will of the donor, shall be
used to contribute to the comfort, convenience,
and enjoyment of the residents of the Decoto
Home.
Alida O Meserve Trust Fund
The principal of this fund is to be used for
playgrounds, playground equipment, and other
comparable forms of amusement for the boys
at Covina.
Minnie E Peterson Fund
The principal of this fund is held by the
Homes subject to a life annuity.
Ralph Walter Kanz and Russell Joseph Kanz Trusts
The ~rincipal and income of these trusts shall
be used for the education of the two named
beneficiaries, subject to the discretion of
the trustees. When both beneficiaries have
completed or abandoned their education or
reached age 27, the trust estate remaining
shall be distributed to the Masonic Homes of
California.
The F C Hardy Memorial for Higher Practical Education
The net income from this trust is to be used
for higher practical education.
The Roy G Jones Trust Fund
All income from this trust is to be paid when
received to a beneficiary for the duration of
her life. Masonic Homes of California holds
a 50 % remainder interest in the assets.

REPORT OF CERTIFIED PUBLIC ACCOUNTANTS
MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNIA
NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
June 30, 1975 and 1974

4 - Pensions
The Masonic Homes contributes to the California Masonic
Retirement Plan for the benefit of substantially all full-time
employees. The total pension exI?ense for the years ended June 30,
1975 and 1974 was approximately $69,300 and $72,000, respectively.
All prior service and current service costs have been funded.
Assets held by fund at December 31, 1974 were in excess of vested
benefits.

SUPPLEMENTARY FINANCIAL INFORMATION

The accompanying schedules included hereinafter, although
not necessary for a fair presentation of the assets, liabilities,
reserves, and fund balances arising from cash transactions of
Masonic Homes of California at June 30, 1975 and 1974 or the related
revenues and expenses for the years then ended, are presented as
supplementary information.

Such schedules have been subjected to

the auditing procedures applied in our examinations of the financial
statements and are, in our opinion, presented fairly in all material
respects when considered in relation to the financial statements
taken as a whole.

Certified Public Accountants

CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
June 30, 1975 and 1974

l - Significant Accounting Policies
Basis of Accounting
The financial statements are presented on a modified
cash basis of accounting. Generally, revenues ·are
recorded at the time of ·receipt and expenses are
recorded when paid. Insurance premiums covering
certain three-year policies are charged to expense
ratably over the policy term.
Land, Buildings, and Equipment
Land, buildings, and equipment are carried at cost
and, except for land, are depreciated on the
straight-line method over estimated useful lives of
50 years for Temple building and equipment, 20 years
for furnishings, and 10 years for sound and lighting
equipment. Maintenance and repairs of a minor
nature are charged to expense when paid. Renewals
of a major nature, which extend the useful lives of
the land, buildings, and equipment, are capitalized.
On sale or retirement, the cost and accumulated
depreciation applicable thereto is eliminated from
the books and the difference between· net book value
and the proceeds from sale or retirement is included
in income.
Investments
Investments in securities purchased are carried at
cost and securities received by gift or bequest are
carried at approximate market value on the date
received.
Federal and State Income Taxes
The Temple is exempt from Federal anQ state income
taxes.

3 - Special Feasibility Study
A special feasibility study authorized at the 1971 annual
communication was completed at a total cost of $54,500. Of this
amount, $39,500 was charged to expense in the year ended June 30, 1973
and $15,000, which is recoverable if the same architect is engaged for
continuance of the project, is carried on the balance sheet as a
deposit.

4 - Pension Plan
The Temple contributes to the California Masonic Retirement
Plan for the benefit of all eligible employees. Total pension costs
were $375 in 1975 and $1,207 in 1974. All prior and current service
costs have been funded. Assets held by the Fund at December 31, 1974
were in excess of vested benefits.

We ha ve examined the statements of assets, liabilities and
fund balances arising from cash transactions of California Masonic
Foundation, a nonprofit corporation, at June 30, 1975 and 1974 and
the related statements of revenues and expenses for the years then
ended. Our examinations were made in accordance with generally
accepted auditing standards, and accordingly included such tests of
the accounting records and such other auditing procedures as we
considered necessary in the circumstances.
The market value of general fund common stock investments
was approximately $64,000 or 57% below their carrying value as of
June 30, 1975· • It is not determinable whether this decline is of a
temporary or permanent nature. Any decline in the market value of
bonds is considered temporary since it is generally the policy of the
trustees to hold bonds until maturity.
In our opinion, subject to the ultimate realization of the
carrying value of common stocks, the financial statements identified
above present fairly the assets, liabilities and fund balances arising
from cash transactions of California Masonic Foundation at June 30,
1975 and 1974 and revenues and expenses for the years then ended, on
a consistent basis.

CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION
NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
June 30, 1975 and 1974

3 - Altenburg Fund
1 -

Significant Accounting Policies

This fund is used to provide loans to students.

Basis of Accounting
The financial statements are presented on a
modified cash basis of accounting. Generally,
revenues are recorded at the time of receipt and
expenses are recorded when paid. The Federal
excise tax on private foundations is accrued as
an expense of the year for which it is incurred.
Investments
Investments in securities purchased are carried
at cost and securities received by gift or
bequest are carried at approximate market value
on the date received.
Federal Excise Tax
The Foundation is exempt from Federal and state
income taxes but is subject to a 4% excise tax
on its net investment income.

2 - Note Receivable
The note receivable held by the General Fund is secured by
a deed of trust on real property and is collectible in installments to
February 1988 with interest at 7-1/2%.
The note receivable held by the Amaranth Fund is also secured
by a deed of trust and is due in installments to October 1980 with
interest at 7-1/2%.

4 - Amaranth Fund
The assets of this fund are restricted by a trust agreement
with the Amaranth Homes of California which specifies that the
principal is to be invested and that the income is to be used to provide
educational grants to women under age 21.
